lessons.title: Signed impulse, direct impact and energy
lessons.summary: Use a signed momentum balance, identify the system and separate restitution from energy conservation.
lessons.objective: Determine every signed post-impact velocity and impulse, and test restitution and energy against the physical conditions.
lessons.before: Use signed components and exact fractions confidently. Review components and direction conventions. Kinetic energy is one half of mass times speed squared; speed is the magnitude of velocity.
lessons.ideas:
Momentum and impulse are vectors

For a particle of constant mass, momentum is mass times velocity. The impulse of the resultant force equals the change in momentum. An impulse may reverse velocity even when its duration is very short.

\[\begin{gathered}\mathbf p=m\mathbf v\\\mathbf J=\int\mathbf F\,dt=m(\mathbf v-\mathbf u)\\\mathbf F_{\rm mean}=\frac{\mathbf J}{\Delta t}\end{gathered}\]

State the positive direction before writing scalar components. If a velocity changes from +5 to −2, its change is −7, not −3. A negative impulse describes direction; its magnitude is positive.

Choose the system before conserving momentum

For two colliding particles, their contact impulses are equal and opposite. Adding their individual momentum changes cancels those internal impulses. Total momentum is conserved only in a direction where the external impulse on the chosen system is negligible. A wall exerts an external impulse on a sphere, so the sphere's normal momentum is not conserved.

\[\begin{gathered}m_Au_A+m_Bu_B=m_Av_A+m_Bv_B\end{gathered}\]

Restitution uses relative velocities

In a direct impact put A to the left of B and take rightwards as positive. For an actual approaching contact, \(u_A-u_B>0\). The non-negative speed of separation is \(v_{B}\)−\(v_{A}\). Newton's experimental law is

\[\begin{gathered}v_B-v_A=e(u_A-u_B)\\0\le e\le1\end{gathered}\]

Use the same signs in the momentum equation. Do not insert the two individual speeds into the restitution equation without checking their directions. Solving the two linear equations gives

\[\begin{gathered}v_A=\frac{m_Au_A+m_Bu_B-m_Be(u_A-u_B)}{m_A+m_B}\\v_B=\frac{m_Au_A+m_Bu_B+m_Ae(u_A-u_B)}{m_A+m_B}\end{gathered}\]

Energy is a separate calculation

Write the initial and final kinetic energies using squared signed velocities. Substituting the momentum and restitution results into their difference gives

\[\begin{gathered}K_{\rm before}-K_{\rm after}=\frac{m_Am_B}{2(m_A+m_B)}(1-e^2)(u_A-u_B)^2\end{gathered}\]

The expression is non-negative for physical e. Only \(e=1\) gives no loss in an actual impact with a positive approach speed. An individual sphere can gain kinetic energy while the pair loses energy. At \(e=0\) the two direct post-impact velocities agree instantaneously; permanent attachment requires a separate physical assumption.

Inverse observations must be admissible

A statement that A rebounds is a sign condition on \(v_{A}\), not merely a positive speed. Solve the observation together with the impact equations, then check \(0\le e\le1\), a positive approach speed and the stated direction. If no admissible value remains, explain that the observation is incompatible with this model.
lessons.method:
1. Draw the pre-impact order and choose a positive direction.
  2. Choose the system and state why its external impulse is negligible in the required direction.
  3. Write signed momentum conservation and relative separation = e × relative approach.
  4. Solve for every requested velocity, then obtain impulse from \(m(v-u)\).
  5. Check the directions, the restitution interval and the total kinetic-energy change.
mistakes: Momentum uses signed velocities, whereas kinetic energy uses their squares.
Restitution relates relative velocities, not the speeds of one sphere alone.
A rebound means a reversal of direction.
A gain in one sphere’s energy need not be a gain for the pair.
An algebraic value of e outside [0,1] is not physical in this model.

examples.title: 1 · A vector impulse and its mean force
examples.question: A 2 kg particle changes velocity from \((3,-1)\) to \((-1,5)\) m s⁻¹ during 0.3 s. Find both components of the impulse, its magnitude and both components of the mean resultant force.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mathbf J=2\bigl((-1,5)-(3,-1)\bigr)=(-8,12)\\|\mathbf J|=\sqrt{(-8)^2+12^2}\\\mathbf F_{\rm mean}=\frac{\mathbf J}{3/10}\end{gathered}\]

Retain the negative horizontal component. A force magnitude alone would not specify its direction.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}J_x=-8\\J_y=12\\|\mathbf J|=4 \sqrt{13}\\F_x=- \frac{80}{3}\\F_y=40\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 2 · Two signed velocities and the loss of energy
examples.question: Sphere A, mass 2 kg, is to the left of sphere B, mass 3 kg, on a smooth line. Their approaching velocities are +7 and −1 m s⁻¹. The restitution coefficient is 1/2. Find both velocities after impact, the impulse on A and the total loss of kinetic energy.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}2v_A+3v_B=11\\v_B-v_A=4\end{gathered}\]

Solve the two equations. A has a negative post-impact velocity, so it rebounds. The impulse on A is 2(\(v_{A}\)−7). The energy-loss formula uses the approach speed 8.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}v_A=- \frac{1}{5}\\v_B=\frac{19}{5}\\J_A=- \frac{72}{5}\\K_{\rm lost}=\frac{144}{5}\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 3 · A rebound interval and a stopping observation
examples.question: A 2 kg sphere A approaches a stationary 3 kg sphere B with velocity +6 m s⁻¹. Find the complete physical interval of e for which A rebounds. Also find e and B’s velocity when A is instantaneously at rest after impact.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v_A=\frac{12-18e}{5}\\v_B=\frac{12+12e}{5}\\v_A\lt0\iff e\gt\frac23\end{gathered}\]

Intersect the strict rebound condition with \(0\le e\le1\): the interval is (2/3,1]. The boundary is a stop, not a rebound. Setting \(v_{A}\)=0 fixes that boundary value and then B’s velocity.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}e_{\rm stop}=\frac{2}{3}\\v_{B,\rm stop}=4\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 4 · One sphere gains energy
examples.question: On a smooth line, a 1 kg sphere A approaches a 2 kg sphere B with signed velocities +6 and −1 m s⁻¹. The coefficient of restitution is 1/2. Find the post-impact velocities and compare the energy lost by A with the energy gained by B.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v_A+2v_B=4\\v_B-v_A=\frac72\end{gathered}\]

A loses \(18-\frac12=\frac{35}2\) J. B gains \(\frac{25}4-1=\frac{21}4\) J. Thus the ratio of A’s loss to B’s gain is 10:3, and the total loss is their difference. Do not add a gain as though it were another loss.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}v_A=-1\\v_B=\frac{5}{2}\\L_A=\frac{35}{2}\\G_B=\frac{21}{4}\\\frac{L_A}{G_B}=\frac{10}{3}\\K_{\rm lost}=\frac{49}{4}\end{gathered}\]

lessons.title: Smooth fixed surfaces and rebound geometry
lessons.summary: Resolve normal and tangential velocities; connect the rebound to angles, energy and the next flight.
lessons.objective: Apply a smooth-surface impulse to the normal component only and reconstruct the full post-impact motion.
lessons.before: Use the signed impulse and restitution equations. Review dot products, unit vectors and projectile trajectories. A wall or ground is fixed in this model.
lessons.ideas:
The contact geometry chooses the components

Take a unit normal n pointing from the surface into the region accessible to the particle. An incoming velocity has \(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n<0\). Smooth contact supplies no tangential impulse, so the tangential velocity stays unchanged. Restitution reverses and scales the normal component:

\[\begin{gathered}u_n=\mathbf u\mathbin{\cdot}\mathbf n\\v_n=-eu_n\\\mathbf v=\mathbf u-(1+e)(\mathbf u\mathbin{\cdot}\mathbf n)\mathbf n\end{gathered}\]

This vector rule is useful for an inclined wall because its normal need not be a coordinate axis. Check that n has length one. Momentum of the particle in the normal direction changes: the fixed support supplies the impulse. Tangential momentum is conserved for the particle because that impulse has zero tangential component.

Impulse and energy loss

\[\begin{gathered}\mathbf J=-m(1+e)u_n\mathbf n\\K_{\rm lost}=\frac12m(1-e^2)u_n^2\end{gathered}\]

Only the normal component contributes to the loss. Squaring the full initial speed in the loss formula would incorrectly remove tangential energy. At \(e=0\) the normal velocity becomes zero, but a nonzero tangential component remains: the particle need not stop.

Angles need a named reference line

If the incoming and outgoing paths make acute angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) with the surface, their tangent-to-normal components give

\[\begin{gathered}\tan\alpha=\frac{|u_n|}{|u_t|}\\\tan\beta=\frac{|v_n|}{|v_t|}=e\tan\alpha\end{gathered}\]

If the angles are measured from the normal, use the reciprocal ratios instead. Draw the outgoing direction before using a tangent. A perpendicular final path is a vector dot-product condition; a parallel final path is a determinant condition. These are conditions on whole velocity vectors.

A rebound can start a new projectile stage

At a smooth horizontal ground, the horizontal velocity is unchanged and the upward rebound velocity is e times the downward impact speed. Gravity acts over the following flight. With upward launch speed w and gravity g, solving \(y=wt-\frac12gt^2\) gives the next positive ground-contact time \(\frac{2w}{g}\) and maximum height \(\frac{w^2}{2g}\). A vertical velocity component is continuous during free flight but changes impulsively at contact.

Find the first reachable surface

For several surfaces, calculate each positive candidate contact time from the current position and velocity. Reject contacts outside a finite wall segment and contacts on its inaccessible side. Use the earliest physical event. If two contacts are simultaneous, a sequence of two separate single-wall models has not been justified; either exclude that case or supply an explicit multiple-contact model.
lessons.method:
1. Choose a unit normal into the allowed region and a perpendicular unit tangent.
  2. Resolve the incoming velocity and confirm that its normal component is negative.
  3. Keep the tangential component; replace the normal component by −e times its old value.
  4. Reconstruct both Cartesian components and calculate impulse or energy using the normal change.
  5. Apply the next stage of motion only until its first reachable event.
mistakes: Smoothness preserves tangential velocity, not the whole velocity.
The particle’s normal momentum is not conserved at a fixed wall.
State whether an angle is measured from the surface or its normal.
\(e=0\) does not stop a particle that still has tangential velocity.
Do not select an event at negative time or silently order simultaneous contacts.

examples.title: 1 · A vertical wall changes one component
examples.question: A 2 kg particle approaches the wall x=0 from x>0 with velocity \((-6,8)\) m s⁻¹. The wall is smooth and \(e=\frac{3}{4}\). Find the outgoing velocity, impulse, speed and energy loss.
examples.solution:
The allowed-region normal is (1,0). The horizontal velocity becomes −(3/4)(−6)=9/2; the vertical component stays 8. Subtract the two complete velocities to find impulse.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}v_x=\frac{9}{2}\\v_y=8\\J_x=21\\J_y=0\\|\mathbf v|=\frac{\sqrt{337}}{2}\\K_{\rm lost}=\frac{63}{4}\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 2 · An inclined wall in vector form
examples.question: The allowed side of a smooth fixed line has inward unit normal \(\mathbf n=(3/5,4/5)\). A 3 kg particle arrives with velocity \((-5,-5)\) m s⁻¹ and \(e=\frac{3}{7}\). Find its outgoing velocity and impulse, and the energy lost.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}u_n=(-5)\frac35+(-5)\frac45=-7\\\mathbf v=\mathbf u+10\mathbf n=(1,3)\end{gathered}\]

A unit tangent (−4/5,3/5) gives tangential velocity 1 both before and after impact. The change (6,8) is wholly normal to the line.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}v_x=1\\v_y=3\\J_x=18\\J_y=24\\K_{\rm lost}=60\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 3 · Recover restitution from the rebound speed
examples.question: A 4 kg particle approaches x=0 from the right with velocity \((-8,6)\) m s⁻¹. After smooth impact its speed is \(2\sqrt{13}\) m s⁻¹. Find e, both outgoing components and the energy loss; give the tangent of the acute outgoing angle \(\beta\) to the wall.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v_x=8e,\qquad v_y=6\\64e^2+36=52\end{gathered}\]

The admissible non-negative root is \(e=\frac{1}{2}\). The outgoing angle is measured from the vertical wall, so tan \(\beta\)=\(v_{x}\)/|\(v_{y}\)|=2/3.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}e=\frac{1}{2}\\v_x=4\\v_y=6\\\tan\beta=\frac{2}{3}\\K_{\rm lost}=96\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 4 · A ground rebound followed by free flight
examples.question: A particle of mass 1/2 kg strikes smooth horizontal ground with velocity \((4,-9)\) m s⁻¹, taking upward as positive. Let \(e=\frac{2}{3}\) and g=10 m s⁻². Treat contact as instantaneous and neglect the impulse of gravity during it. Find its rebound velocity, the next flight time, maximum height, horizontal range and upward ground impulse.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v_x=4,\qquad v_y=6\\y=6t-5t^2\\0=y\Longrightarrow t=0\ \hbox{or}\ t=\frac65\end{gathered}\]

The positive root is the next ground contact. The apex occurs at t=3/5. The ground impulse is the vertical momentum change; gravity over the subsequent flight is not part of this impact impulse.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}v_x=4\\v_y=6\\T=\frac{6}{5}\\H=\frac{9}{5}\\R=\frac{24}{5}\\J_y=\frac{15}{2}\end{gathered}\]

lessons.title: Oblique impacts between smooth spheres
lessons.summary: Apply the two-particle impact equations along the line of centres and preserve each tangential velocity separately.
lessons.objective: Recover complete outgoing velocity vectors and solve inverse impact conditions without losing the geometry.
lessons.before: Use direct-impact equations and normal and tangential resolution. Here both spheres can move, so use pair momentum along the contact normal rather than the fixed-wall rule.
lessons.ideas:
The line of centres is the impulse direction

At contact let n be a unit vector from A’s centre to B’s centre, and take t perpendicular to n. For smooth spheres the impulsive contact force acts along n. Each sphere therefore keeps its own tangential velocity; the two normal velocities obey the same momentum and restitution equations as a direct impact.

\[\begin{gathered}u_{An}=\mathbf u_A\cdot\mathbf n,\qquad u_{Bn}=\mathbf u_B\cdot\mathbf n\\m_Au_{An}+m_Bu_{Bn}=m_Av_{An}+m_Bv_{Bn}\\v_{Bn}-v_{An}=e(u_{An}-u_{Bn})\\v_{At}=u_{At},\qquad v_{Bt}=u_{Bt}\end{gathered}\]

The approach condition is \(u_{An}-u_{Bn}>0\). An algebraic restitution calculation does not establish that two spheres will actually meet: their centres must be at the contact separation, their paths must reach that configuration and their velocities must be approaching along n.

Reconstruct the whole answer

\[\begin{gathered}\mathbf v_A=v_{An}\mathbf n+u_{At}\mathbf t\\\mathbf v_B=v_{Bn}\mathbf n+u_{Bt}\mathbf t\end{gathered}\]

Reporting only \(v_{An}\) and \(v_{Bn}\) does not give the two outgoing velocities in the plane. The same basis must be used for both particles; reversing a tangent halfway through changes a sign. In Cartesian coordinates an equivalent update is \(v_{A}\)=\(u_{A}\)+(\(v_{An}\)−\(u_{An}\))n, with the analogous expression for B.

Impulse and kinetic energy

\[\begin{gathered}\mathbf J_A=m_A(v_{An}-u_{An})\mathbf n=-\mathbf J_B\\K_{\rm lost}=\frac{m_Am_B}{2(m_A+m_B)}(1-e^2)(u_{An}-u_{Bn})^2\end{gathered}\]

The tangential energies cancel from the loss because neither tangential component changes. Thus a small normal approach speed can mean a small loss even when the spheres’ total speeds are large.

Use vector conditions in inverse problems

For perpendicular outgoing paths require \(\mathbf v_A\cdot\mathbf v_B=0\). For parallel nonzero outgoing paths require their two-dimensional determinant to vanish, then distinguish the same and opposite directions if needed. Solve the scalar condition together with \(0\le e\le1\), positive masses and the approaching-contact condition. Check each root in the original vector equations.

Zero restitution is not automatic attachment

When \(e=0\) the normal relative velocity is zero immediately after impact. The tangential relative velocity can still be nonzero, so the two complete velocities need not agree. Do not replace the pair by one permanently joined body unless attachment is explicitly stated. These translational smooth-contact equations make no claim about spin or frictional impulses.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the actual contact normal from the line of centres and choose a unit tangent.
  2. Resolve both initial velocities and check the positive normal approach speed.
  3. Solve pair momentum and restitution for the two signed normal velocities.
  4. Keep each sphere’s tangential component and reconstruct all Cartesian components.
  5. Apply any path constraint to the complete vectors; check e, geometry and energy.
mistakes: A smooth sphere’s tangential component stays with that sphere, not with the pair average.
The fixed-wall rule \(v_{n}\)=−eu_n does not apply to two movable spheres.
The relative normal approach speed differs from the magnitude of the relative velocity.
An inverse root must still lie in [0,1].
Equal normal velocities at \(e=0\) do not imply equal full velocities or attachment.

examples.title: 1 · An axis-aligned line of centres
examples.question: At contact A is to the left of B and the line of centres is horizontal. Their masses are 2 kg and 1 kg; the incoming velocities are \((6,3)\) and \((-2,-1)\) m s⁻¹. Let \(e=\frac{1}{2}\). Find both complete outgoing velocities, the impulse on A and the total energy loss.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}2v_{Ax}+v_{Bx}=10\\v_{Bx}-v_{Ax}=4\\v_{Ay}=3,\qquad v_{By}=-1\end{gathered}\]

Resolve the contact impulse horizontally. The vertical components remain with their original spheres and are not averaged.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}v_{Ax}=2\\v_{Ay}=3\\v_{Bx}=6\\v_{By}=-1\\J_{Ax}=-8\\K_{\rm lost}=16\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 2 · A tilted contact normal
examples.question: At contact the unit normal from a 1 kg sphere A towards a 2 kg sphere B is \((3/5,4/5)\). Their velocities before contact are \((7/5,26/5)\) and \((-3,1)\) m s⁻¹. Let \(e=\frac{1}{2}\). Find both outgoing velocity vectors and the magnitude of A’s impulse.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mathbf t=(-4/5,3/5)\\(u_{An},u_{At})=(5,2)\\(u_{Bn},u_{Bt})=(-1,3)\\v_{An}+2v_{Bn}=3\\v_{Bn}-v_{An}=3\end{gathered}\]

The normal results are −1 and 2. Recombine them with tangential components 2 and 3. The impulse on A has normal component −6 and zero tangential component.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}v_{Ax}=- \frac{11}{5}\\v_{Ay}=\frac{2}{5}\\v_{Bx}=- \frac{6}{5}\\v_{By}=\frac{17}{5}\\|\mathbf J_A|=6\\K_{\rm lost}=9\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 3 · Perpendicular outgoing paths determine e
examples.question: Two equal 1 kg spheres touch with a horizontal line of centres, A to the left. Before impact their velocities are \((5,2)\) and \((0,-2)\) m s⁻¹. Find e if their outgoing paths are perpendicular, then give both outgoing velocities.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v_{Ax}=\frac52(1-e),\qquad v_{Bx}=\frac52(1+e)\\\mathbf v_A\cdot\mathbf v_B=\frac{25}{4}(1-e^2)-4=0\end{gathered}\]

The non-negative physical root is 3/5. Substitute it back before reporting the whole vectors. Their dot product is \(1\times4+2\times(-2)=0\).

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}e=\frac{3}{5}\\v_{Ax}=1\\v_{Ay}=2\\v_{Bx}=4\\v_{By}=-2\\K_{\rm lost}=4\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 4 · Equal normal velocities, different trajectories
examples.question: A 2 kg sphere A is to the left of a 3 kg sphere B at a horizontal contact. The incoming velocities are \((5,4)\) and \((0,-1)\) m s⁻¹ and \(e=0\). Find both outgoing velocities and the energy loss. Do the smooth-sphere equations imply that they remain joined?
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v_{Ax}=v_{Bx}=\frac{2(5)+3(0)}5=2\end{gathered}\]

The tangential components stay 4 and −1. Thus the complete velocities differ; permanent joining does not follow. The tangential relative motion also means that equal instantaneous normal components must not be read as identical trajectories.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}v_{Ax}=2\\v_{Ay}=4\\v_{Bx}=2\\v_{By}=-1\\J_{Ax}=-6\\K_{\rm lost}=15\end{gathered}\]

lessons.title: Successive impacts and deciding the next event
lessons.summary: Carry the current state from one event to the next, and distinguish finite stages from a limiting infinite sequence.
lessons.objective: Determine the chronological sequence of contacts and the complete post-impact states, with valid stopping or limiting conditions.
lessons.before: Use direct impacts, wall impacts and simple geometric series. Treat the particles as small point models for the stated separation calculations; finite sphere radii would require corresponding contact distances.
lessons.ideas:
A fresh momentum equation at every contact

For an isolated pair impact use the two particles that are actually touching. A third particle’s velocity is unchanged during that contact when it receives no impulse. The output velocities become the next stage’s input velocities. Do not conserve the pair’s kinetic energy unless that impact is perfectly elastic.

Positions decide whether another contact occurs

Between impacts, uniform trajectories have the form \(x_i=x_{i0}+v_i t\). For two separated particles solve \(x_A=x_B\) for the next positive time. If A is behind B, A can catch it only if \(v_A>v_B\) in that coordinate direction. Equal velocities with a positive gap keep that gap; a faster particle moving away cannot be caught.

\[\begin{gathered}\Delta t=\frac{x_B-x_A}{v_A-v_B}\quad\hbox{when A is behind B and }v_A\gt v_B\end{gathered}\]

List all competing positive event times: another pair contact, a wall contact or a return to a named point. Select the earliest physically reachable event. A zero-time candidate may be the contact just processed, rather than another impact. Simultaneous three-body contacts are outside a sequence of separate two-body impact equations unless a model for them is supplied.

A wall changes the state before the return journey

First propagate both positions to the wall-impact time. Change the striking particle’s normal velocity using the wall’s restitution coefficient, then solve the new relative-motion problem. A relative speed calculated before the rebound is not the closing speed afterwards.

Repeated rebounds give geometric sequences

For vertical rebounds on smooth fixed horizontal ground with constant e in (0,1), let w be the upward velocity immediately after the current impact. The subsequent upward launch velocities are \(w,ew,e^2w,\ldots\); their maximum heights have ratio \(e^2\). The sum of all forthcoming flight times and the sum of vertical distances are

\[\begin{gathered}T_\infty=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{2we^n}{g}=\frac{2w}{g(1-e)}\\S_\infty=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{w^2e^{2n}}{g}=\frac{w^2}{g(1-e^2)}\end{gathered}\]

These are limits of an idealised infinite sequence. They do not mean that a particular finite bounce has zero speed. A physical model for settling is needed beyond the accumulation limit. At \(e=1\) these series do not converge; at \(e=0\) there is no upward next flight after a downward impact.

Several fixed surfaces

Apply the normal/tangential rule in each surface’s own basis. At perpendicular walls, each impact changes one Cartesian component, but the first wall still has to be determined from the geometry. Sum the separate impulses as vectors if a total impulse is requested. Momentum of the particle alone is not conserved across its contacts with the supports.
lessons.method:
1. Record every current position, signed velocity and relevant restitution coefficient.
  2. Calculate all positive candidate contact times and choose the first valid event.
  3. Propagate every particle to that time, then solve only the actual impact.
  4. Repeat with the new state; justify any claim that no further collision occurs.
  5. For an infinite sequence, identify exactly what is being summed and state the admissible range of e.
mistakes: The next pair in the spatial order is not automatically the next pair to collide.
Propagate the other particle while one particle travels to a wall.
A zero-time solution may be the impact already processed.
Successive speeds scale by e, but successive rebound heights scale by \(e^2\).
A limiting total time is not the time of a last finite bounce.

examples.title: 1 · Two contacts, then a persistent gap
examples.question: Three equal 1 kg particles A, B and C lie on a smooth line. At time 0 A strikes B at x=0, while C is at rest at x=6 m. Just before the first impact A has velocity +8 m s⁻¹ and B is at rest. Let \(e_{AB}=\frac12\) and \(e_{BC}=\frac13\). Find the next contact time and all velocities just after it. Show whether A can catch B afterwards.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v_A=2,\qquad v_B=6\quad\hbox{after the first impact}\\\Delta t=6/6=1\\x_A(1)=2,\qquad x_B(1)=x_C(1)=6\end{gathered}\]

During the second contact only B and C exchange impulse. Their outgoing velocities are 2 and 4. A and B then have equal velocities while separated by 4 m, so they do not meet again; C moves away faster.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}T=1\\x_{BC}=6\\v_A=2\\v_B=2\\v_C=4\\d_{AB}=4\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 2 · A wall rebound creates a later meeting
examples.question: Immediately after separating at x=0, two equal 1 kg particles A and B have velocities +1 and +4 m s⁻¹ on a smooth line. A wall is at x=6 m and its restitution coefficient with B is 1/2. Find the time and position of their next mutual contact, measured from separation. Their mutual coefficient is 1/2; find both velocities immediately after that contact.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}t_{\rm wall}=\frac64=\frac32\\x_A(t_{\rm wall})=\frac32,\qquad v_B=-2\\\Delta t=\frac{6-3/2}{1-(-2)}=\frac32\end{gathered}\]

The next contact therefore occurs at absolute time 3 and position 3. Use incoming velocities +1 and −2 in a fresh equal-mass impact. The calculation stops just after this contact; it does not assert that no future wall contact can occur.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}t_{\rm wall}=\frac{3}{2}\\T=3\\x_{AB}=3\\v_A=- \frac{5}{4}\\v_B=\frac{1}{4}\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 3 · A convergent ideal rebound sequence
examples.question: A ball is released from rest 5 m above smooth horizontal ground. Let g=10 m s⁻² and let every ground impact have \(e=\frac{1}{2}\). Find the formal accumulation time measured from release, and the total distance in the idealised infinite sequence.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}U=\sqrt{2(10)(5)}=10,\qquad t_{\rm first}=1\\w=5\\T_\infty=1+\frac{2(5)}{10(1-1/2)}\\S_\infty=5+\frac{5^2}{10(1-1/4)}\end{gathered}\]

The initial downward distance and initial fall time are counted once. Every later flight travels both upwards and downwards. The finite sum is a model limit, not the end of a numbered final bounce.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}T_\infty=3\\S_\infty=\frac{25}{3}\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 4 · Decide the first wall before changing components
examples.question: A 2 kg particle starts at (0,0) with velocity (6,8) m s⁻¹. It is confined by the smooth lines x=9 and y=8 to x≤9, y≤8. Both restitution coefficients are 1/2. Find the first two contact times, the position and velocity after the second contact, the combined impulse and the energy lost.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}t_y=8/8=1,\qquad t_x=9/6=\frac32\end{gathered}\]

The horizontal wall is first. At time 1 the particle is at (6,8) and its velocity becomes (6,−4). It reaches x=9 after a further half-second, at (9,6), where the horizontal component changes to −3. The contacts are distinct; no corner rule is needed.

Hence the complete result is

\[\begin{gathered}t_1=1\\t_2=\frac{3}{2}\\x_2=9\\y_2=6\\v_x=-3\\v_y=-4\\J_x=-18\\J_y=-24\\K_{\rm lost}=75\end{gathered}\]

questions.title: Both outgoing velocities, impulse and energy
questions.prompt_html: At an approaching direct contact A is to the left of B. Rightwards is positive. Let \(m_A=2,\ m_B=1\) kg, \(u_A=6,\ u_B=-3\) m s⁻¹ and \(e=\frac{1}{3}\). Give both signed outgoing velocities, the signed impulse on A and the total energy loss.

questions.title: One sphere gains energy while the pair loses energy
questions.prompt_html:
Two small smooth spheres \(A\) and \(B\), of masses \(4m\) and \(3m\), move on a smooth horizontal surface. Take rightwards as positive. Immediately before a direct impact their velocities are \(2u\) and \(-u\), respectively, where \(u\gt 0\). The coefficient of restitution is \(e\).

  1. Find the signed velocities \(v_A,v_B\) immediately after impact in terms of \(u,e\).

    [4]

  2. It is observed that \(A\) rebounds with speed \(u/7\). Find \(e\).

    [2]

  3. For this impact, find the ratio of the kinetic energy lost by \(A\) to the kinetic energy gained by \(B\). State whether the total kinetic energy increases or decreases.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v_A=(5-9e)u/7,\quad v_B=(5+12e)u/7\).

(b)

\(e=2/3\).

(c)

The ratio is \(13:6\); the pair loses \(30mu^2/7\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

During the impact the total horizontal impulse from outside the pair is negligible. Momentum and restitution give \[4v_A+3v_B=4(2u)+3(-u)=5u,\qquad v_B-v_A=3eu.\] Substitute \(v_B=v_A+3eu\) into the first equation: \(7v_A+9eu=5u\). Hence \[v_A=\frac{5-9e}{7}u,\qquad v_B=\frac{5+12e}{7}u.\] The sign of \(v_A\) must be retained; its speed is \(|v_A|\).

Part (b)

Rebound means \(v_A=-u/7\), not \(+u/7\). Thus \(5-9e=-1\), giving \(e=2/3\), which lies in \([0,1]\). Then \(v_B=13u/7\).

Part (c)

For \(A\), \[L_A=\frac12(4m)\left[(2u)^2-(u/7)^2\right]=\frac{390}{49}mu^2.\] For \(B\), \[G_B=\frac12(3m)\left[(13u/7)^2-u^2\right]=\frac{180}{49}mu^2.\] Thus \(L_A:G_B=390:180=13:6\). The pair loses \(L_A-G_B=30mu^2/7\gt 0\). An individual sphere can gain energy even though the total decreases.
questions.hint_html: Use signed velocities first. A loss for the pair does not require both spheres to lose kinetic energy.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the ratio and correct total-energy conclusion.

questions.title: An energy observation with two algebraic roots
questions.prompt_html:
Identical smooth spheres \(A,B\), each of mass \(m\), approach one another on a smooth horizontal line with velocities \(u\) and \(-ku\), where \(u,k\gt 0\). In the impact \(B\) is brought to rest. The coefficient of restitution is \(e\).

  1. Express \(e\) in terms of \(k\) and state the resulting restriction on \(k\).

    [3]

  2. Exactly \(80\%\) of the total initial kinetic energy is lost. Find \(k\) and \(e\).

    [4]

  3. For the value found, determine the impulse on \(B\), including its direction.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(e=(k-1)/(k+1)\), with \(k\geq1\).

(b)

\(k=2,\quad e=1/3\).

(c)

\(2mu\), in the original direction of \(A\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Momentum gives the final velocity of \(A\) as \((1-k)u\). The relative velocity of separation is therefore \(0-(1-k)u=(k-1)u\), whereas the approach speed is \((1+k)u\). Thus \(e=(k-1)/(k+1)\). Non-negative \(e\) requires \(k\geq1\); for finite positive \(k\) the fraction is less than 1.

Part (b)

The initial energy is \(mu^2(1+k^2)/2\), and the final energy is \(mu^2(1-k)^2/2\). The retained fraction is \(1/5\), so \[\frac{(1-k)^2}{1+k^2}=\frac15,\qquad 2k^2-5k+2=0.\] Hence \((2k-1)(k-2)=0\), giving \(k=1/2\) or \(2\). The former contradicts \(k\geq1\) and would give negative restitution. Thus \(k=2\) and \(e=1/3\).

Part (c)

Sphere \(B\) changes velocity from \(-2u\) to \(0\). Hence its impulse is \(m(0-(-2u))=2mu\), positive in the chosen direction. Sphere \(A\) receives an equal and opposite impulse.
questions.hint_html: Two roots may satisfy the energy equation. Restitution and separation decide which one represents an impact.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the retained fraction, not the lost fraction.

questions.title: A momentum ratio is not a speed ratio
questions.prompt_html:
Two smooth spheres \(A,B\) have masses \(5m,2m\). On a smooth horizontal line, \(A\) moving at speed \(u\) hits the stationary \(B\) directly. After impact both move in the initial direction of \(A\), and the momentum of \(A\) is twice that of \(B\).

  1. Find the coefficient of restitution.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(e=1/6\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let the final velocities be \(a,b\). The momentum ratio gives \(5ma=2(2mb)\), so \(5a=4b\). Conservation gives \(5u=5a+2b=6b\). Hence \(b=5u/6\), \(a=2u/3\). The relative separation speed is \(b-a=u/6\); the approach speed was \(u\). Therefore \(e=1/6\). Both velocities are positive and \(b\gt a\), as required.
questions.hint_html: Twice the momentum does not mean twice the velocity when the masses differ.

questions.title: A threshold for avoiding a third collision
questions.prompt_html:
Three small smooth spheres lie in the order \(A,B,C\) on a straight horizontal line, with positive gaps between neighbouring spheres. Their masses are \(4m,4m,3m\), respectively. Initially \(B,C\) are at rest and \(A\) moves towards \(B\) with speed \(u\). The coefficient of restitution for both impacts is \(e\), where \(0\lt e\leq1\).

  1. Find the velocities of \(A\) and \(B\) immediately after their impact.

    [3]

  2. Find the velocities of \(B\) and \(C\) immediately after the second impact.

    [4]

  3. Find the complete set of \(e\) for which no further impacts occur. Explain whether the lower endpoint is included.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a=(1-e)u/2,\quad b=(1+e)u/2\).

(b)

\(b_2=(4-3e)(1+e)u/14,\quad c=2(1+e)^2u/7\).

(c)

\((4-\sqrt7)/3\leq e\leq1\); the lower endpoint is included.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Take the initial direction of \(A\) as positive. Equal masses give \(a+b=u\), while restitution gives \(b-a=eu\). Adding and subtracting gives \[a=\frac{1-e}{2}u,\qquad b=\frac{1+e}{2}u.\] Since \(e\gt 0\), \(B\) separates from \(A\) and reaches \(C\).

Part (b)

For the second impact, \[4b=4b_2+3c,\qquad c-b_2=eb.\] Eliminating \(c\) gives \(7b_2=(4-3e)b\). Then \(c=4(1+e)b/7\). Substituting the first-impact value of \(b\), \[b_2=\frac{(4-3e)(1+e)}{14}u,\qquad c=\frac{2(1+e)^2}{7}u.\] Both are positive and \(c-b_2=eb\gt 0\).

Part (c)

After the second impact \(A\) is behind \(B\), with a strictly positive gap. Thus no third impact requires \(a\leq b_2\); \(C\) is already separating from \(B\). This yields \[7(1-e)\leq(4-3e)(1+e),\quad 3e^2-8e+3\leq0.\] Its roots are \((4\pm\sqrt7)/3\). Intersecting with \(0\lt e\leq1\) gives the stated interval. At the lower endpoint \(A\) and \(B\) have equal velocities, so their positive gap stays constant: equality does not produce another collision.
questions.hint_html: After two impacts, compare the velocities of adjacent spheres in their spatial order, not merely their speed magnitudes.

marking_criteria.description_html: Restrict to the physical range and justify inclusion of equality.

questions.title: Equal velocities need not mean contact
questions.prompt_html:
Three separated small smooth spheres \(A,B,C\) have masses \(4m,2m,m\), respectively, and are in that order on a smooth horizontal line. Initially only \(A\) moves, with speed \(u\) towards \(B\). The coefficient of restitution is \(e\), with \(0\lt e\leq1\). The first two impacts are \(A\) with \(B\), followed by \(B\) with \(C\).

  1. Find the velocities of all three spheres immediately after the second impact.

    [6]

  2. Immediately after the second impact, \(C\) has twice the speed of \(A\). Find \(e\) and determine whether any further impact occurs.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v_A=(2-e)u/3,\quad v_B=2(2-e)(1+e)u/9,\quad v_C=4(1+e)^2u/9\).

(b)

\(e=1/2\); final velocities are \(u/2,u/2,u\), so no further impact occurs.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Use the original direction of \(A\) as positive. In the first impact, \[4u=4a+2b,\qquad b-a=eu,\] so \(a=(2-e)u/3\), \(b=2(1+e)u/3\).

In the second impact, \[2b=2v_B+v_C,\qquad v_C-v_B=eb.\] Thus \(v_B=(2-e)b/3\) and \(v_C=2(1+e)b/3\). Substitution yields the three expressions. \(A\)’s velocity is unchanged during the second impact.

Part (b)

The velocities in part (a) are non-negative. Hence \[\frac49(1+e)^2=\frac23(2-e),\quad 2e^2+7e-4=0=(2e-1)(e+4).\] Reject \(e=-4\), so \(e=1/2\). Substitution gives \(u/2,u/2,u\). The first two spheres are separated when the second impact occurs and retain their gap; \(C\) moves faster than both. There is no further impact.
questions.hint_html: Keep the velocity from the first impact for \(A\); only \(B\) and \(C\) change at the second.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form and solve the first pair of impact equations.
Give all three final velocities in terms of \(u,e\).
Form the equation from the speed ratio.
Use the ordered velocities and positive gaps to conclude no further impact.

questions.title: A second impact stops the middle sphere
questions.prompt_html:
Three smooth spheres have masses \(3m,6m,2m\) and are labelled \(A,B,C\). They move along the same smooth horizontal line, in that spatial order. Rightwards velocities before any impact are \(2u,-u,-5u/6\), respectively. Their positive separations are such that the first impact is between \(A,B\), followed by an impact between \(B,C\). Both impacts have coefficient of restitution \(e\). The second impact brings \(B\) to rest.

  1. Find the velocities of \(A,B\) immediately after the first impact.

    [4]

  2. Find \(e\) and the velocity of \(C\) after the second impact.

    [3]

  3. Find the total kinetic energy lost in the two impacts.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v_A=-2eu,\quad v_B=eu\).

(b)

\(e=1/2,\quad v_C=2u/3\).

(c)

\(31mu^2/4\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Momentum gives \(3(2u)+6(-u)=3v_A+6v_B=0\), so \(v_A=-2v_B\). Restitution gives \(v_B-v_A=3eu\). Therefore \(3v_B=3eu\), hence \(v_B=eu\), \(v_A=-2eu\).

Part (b)

Since \(B\) stops, momentum for \(B,C\) gives \(6eu-2(5u/6)=2v_C\), or \(v_C=(3e-5/6)u\). Restitution gives \(v_C=e(e+5/6)u\). Equating, \[6e^2-13e+5=0=(2e-1)(3e-5).\] Only \(e=1/2\) is at most 1. It gives \(v_C=2u/3\). The velocities \(-u,0,2u/3\) are separating.

Part (c)

Before either impact, \[K_i=\frac12mu^2\left[3(2)^2+6+2(5/6)^2\right]=\frac{349}{36}mu^2.\] After both, \[K_f=\frac12mu^2\left[3(1)^2+2(2/3)^2\right]=\frac{35}{18}mu^2.\] Thus \(K_i-K_f=(349-70)mu^2/36=31mu^2/4\). The intermediate energy is not counted twice.
questions.hint_html: The first pair has zero total momentum. Use that simplification, but not zero total kinetic energy.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use both laws for the second impact.

questions.title: Can the middle sphere catch the leader?
questions.prompt_html:
Three small smooth spheres \(A,B,C\), in that order, move to the right along a smooth horizontal line with speeds \(3u,u,3u/2\). Their masses are \(m,km,2m\), where \(k\gt 0\). The coefficient of restitution for each pair is \(1/2\). Initially all gaps are positive. Sphere \(A\) catches \(B\).

  1. Find the velocities of \(A,B\) after this impact and the condition on \(k\) for \(B\) subsequently to catch \(C\).

    [4]

  2. For \(k=2\), find the velocities of all three spheres after the first two impacts.

    [4]

  3. Explain why there is no third impact in this case.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a=3u/(1+k),\ b=(k+4)u/(1+k)\); \(0\lt k\lt 5\).

(b)

\(u,13u/8,15u/8\), respectively.

(c)

\(u\lt 13u/8\lt 15u/8\), in the order \(A,B,C\); all gaps increase.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Momentum and restitution give \[a+kb=(3+k)u,\qquad b-a=u.\] Thus \(b=(k+4)u/(1+k)\), \(a=3u/(1+k)\). Sphere \(B\) catches \(C\) only if \(b\gt 3u/2\), since its initial gap from \(C\) is positive. Hence \[2(k+4)\gt 3(k+1),\qquad k\lt 5.\] Together with positive mass, \(0\lt k\lt 5\). At \(k=5\) the gap stays constant, so equality is excluded.

Part (b)

With \(k=2\), \(a=u\), \(b=2u\). The second impact is between equal masses \(2m\), initially moving at \(2u\) and \(3u/2\). If their final velocities are \(b_2,c\), \[b_2+c=\frac72u,\qquad c-b_2=\frac12(2u-3u/2)=\frac14u.\] Thus \(b_2=13u/8\), \(c=15u/8\); \(A\) retains velocity \(u\).

Part (c)

The particles remain ordered \(A,B,C\). Immediately after the second impact, \(B\) moves faster than the trailing \(A\), and \(C\) faster than \(B\). Thus both adjacent gaps increase. No further impact can occur.
questions.hint_html: A sphere cannot catch another one with the same velocity when there is already a positive gap.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the incoming velocities for the second impact.
Conclude from the increasing gaps, not merely positive velocities.

questions.title: A bumper test with a measured contact force
questions.prompt_html:
A small smooth sphere of mass \(0.18\,\mathrm{kg}\) approaches a fixed wall normally at \(18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It rebounds along the same line at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The magnitude of the average contact force during the impact is \(108\,\mathrm N\).

  1. Find the coefficient of restitution.

    [1]

  2. Find the magnitude of the impulse and the duration of contact.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(e=1/3\).

(b)

\(J=4.32\,\mathrm{N\,s}\), \(\Delta t=0.040\,\mathrm s\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

For a fixed wall in a normal impact, \(e\) is rebound speed divided by approach speed: \(e=6/18=1/3\).

Part (b)

Taking motion towards the wall as positive gives \(p_i=0.18(18)\) and \(p_f=0.18(-6)\). Therefore \[\Delta p=0.18(-6-18)=-4.32\,\mathrm{N\,s}.\] The impulse magnitude is \(4.32\,\mathrm{N\,s}\). Since \(J=F_{\rm av}\Delta t\), \(\Delta t=4.32/108=0.040\,\mathrm s\).
questions.hint_html: The velocity reverses. The change in speed magnitude is not the magnitude of the change in velocity.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use opposite signs before and after impact.
Use average force to find the duration.

questions.title: Inferring a rebound speed from a force sensor
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth ball of mass \(0.12\,\mathrm{kg}\) strikes a fixed wall normally at \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Contact lasts \(0.025\,\mathrm s\). The average force exerted by the wall on the ball has magnitude \(84\,\mathrm N\) and points away from the wall. Other impulses during contact are negligible.

  1. Find the speed and direction of the ball immediately after contact.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(5.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), away from the wall.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Take towards the wall as positive. The wall impulse is \(-84(0.025)=-2.1\,\mathrm{N\,s}\). Therefore \[0.12v-0.12(12)=-2.1,\qquad v=-5.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.\] The speed is \(5.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), away from the wall. The corresponding restitution value \(5.5/12=11/24\) is physically admissible.
questions.hint_html: Take the impulse as negative when the incident velocity is positive.

A smooth sphere of unknown mass \(M\,\mathrm{kg}\) strikes a fixed wall normally at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and rebounds at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The contact duration is \(0.060\,\mathrm s\), and the average force from the wall is \(50\,\mathrm N\). Other impulses during the impact are negligible.

(a)

\(M=0.30\).

questions.title: A return from the wall: time and impulse
questions.prompt_html:
Two small smooth spheres \(A,B\) of masses \(3m,2m\) collide directly on a smooth horizontal line. Initially \(A\) has speed \(u\) and \(B\) is at rest. Their coefficient of restitution is \(1/2\). At the first impact their common particle-model position is \(x=0\); a fixed wall is at \(x=d\), with \(d\gt 0\). The wall is perpendicular to the line, and its coefficient of restitution with \(B\) is \(2/3\). Sphere radii are negligible in all travel distances.

  1. Find the velocities of \(A,B\) after the first impact.

    [3]

  2. Find the elapsed time from the first sphere–sphere impact to their next impact.

    [4]

  3. Find the magnitude of the impulse on \(A\) in the second sphere–sphere impact.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(2u/5,\ 9u/10\), both towards the wall.

(b)

\(5d/(3u)\).

(c)

\(9mu/5\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Writing velocities towards the wall as positive, \[3a+2b=3u,\qquad b-a=u/2.\] Substitution gives \(5a=2u\), so \(a=2u/5\), \(b=9u/10\).

Part (b)

Sphere \(B\) reaches the wall at \(t_1=d/b=10d/(9u)\). At that instant \(A\) is at \(at_1=4d/9\), still short of the wall. The separation is \(5d/9\). After rebounding, \(B\)’s velocity is \(-(2/3)b=-3u/5\). The closing speed is \(2u/5+3u/5=u\), so the return-stage time is \(5d/(9u)\). The total is \[\frac{10d}{9u}+\frac{5d}{9u}=\frac{5d}{3u}.\] The meeting point is \(x=a(5d/3u)=2d/3\lt d\), so \(A\) has not hit the wall.

Part (c)

Before the second impact the approach speed is \(u\). If \(J\) is the positive magnitude of the impulse, then \(A\) loses velocity \(J/(3m)\) and \(B\) gains \(J/(2m)\). Restitution requires \[-u+\frac{J}{2m}+\frac{J}{3m}=\frac12u.\] Thus \(5J/(6m)=3u/2\), giving \(J=9mu/5\). The impulse on \(A\) is away from the wall.
questions.hint_html: Draw a timeline: first impact, wall impact, second impact. The total time is not just the return time.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the total time and check the meeting point.
Relate the two velocity changes to a common impulse.

questions.title: A wall rebound determines the restitution
questions.prompt_html:
Sphere \(A\), of mass \(2m\), moving at speed \(u\), collides directly with a stationary sphere \(B\), of mass \(m\), on a smooth horizontal line. The sphere–sphere coefficient of restitution is \(e\), where \(0\lt e\leq1\). Sphere \(B\) next hits a fixed wall perpendicular to the line and rebounds with coefficient \(1/2\). At the subsequent impact between the spheres, \(A\) is brought to rest. Assume the spheres are small compared with their travel distances.

  1. Find the velocities just after the first impact and just before the second sphere–sphere impact.

    [4]

  2. Find \(e\).

    [4]

  3. Determine whether \(B\) will hit the wall again before any further sphere–sphere impact.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

First: \(a=(2-e)u/3,\ b=2(1+e)u/3\). Before the second: \(a,-b/2\).

(b)

\(e=1/2\).

(c)

Yes. Its velocity is \(u/2\) towards the wall, while \(A\) is at rest.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Taking towards the wall as positive gives \(2a+b=2u\) and \(b-a=eu\). Thus \[a=\frac{2-e}{3}u,\qquad b=\frac{2(1+e)}3u.\] After the wall impact \(B\)’s velocity becomes \(-b/2\). Since \(b\gt a\gt 0\) for \(e\gt 0\), \(B\) reaches the wall before \(A\) and returns to meet it.

Part (b)

Let \(w\) be \(B\)’s velocity after the second impact; \(A\)’s is zero. Momentum gives \(w=2a-b/2\), while restitution gives \(w=e(a+b/2)\). Therefore \[(2-e)a=\frac{1+e}{2}b.\] Substituting part (a), \((2-e)^2=(1+e)^2\). Both \(2-e\) and \(1+e\) are positive, hence \(2-e=1+e\), giving \(e=1/2\). Equivalently the difference of squares is \(3(1-2e)\).

Part (c)

At \(e=1/2\), \(a=u/2\), \(b=u\), and \(w=2a-b/2=u/2\). Sphere \(B\) is to the right of \(A\), moving towards the wall; \(A\) remains stationary. Their gap increases until \(B\) reaches the wall. Thus a further wall impact does occur first.
questions.hint_html: Do not set the post-wall velocity equal to \(+b/2\). The wall changes its direction as well as its magnitude.

Use restitution with the sum of approach speeds.

questions.title: Locating the second collision reveals the wall
questions.prompt_html:
Identical small smooth spheres \(A,B\) collide directly at \(x=0\) on a smooth horizontal line. Initially \(A\) has velocity \(u\gt 0\) and \(B\) is at rest. Their coefficient of restitution is \(1/2\). A fixed wall at \(x=d\) is perpendicular to the line. Sphere \(B\) rebounds from it with an unknown coefficient \(r\), where \(0\lt r\leq1\). The spheres next collide at \(x=3d/5\). Model their radii as negligible for travel distances; each sphere has mass \(m\).

  1. Find the velocities after the first impact.

    [3]

  2. Find \(r\) and the time between the two sphere–sphere impacts.

    [4]

  3. Find the kinetic energy lost by \(B\) at the wall and the impulse exerted by the wall on \(B\), giving its direction.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a=u/4,\quad b=3u/4\).

(b)

\(r=1/2,\quad t=12d/(5u)\).

(c)

\(27mu^2/128\); impulse \(9mu/8\) away from the wall.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Momentum gives \(a+b=u\), and restitution gives \(b-a=u/2\). Solving yields \(a=u/4\), \(b=3u/4\).

Part (b)

Since \(A\) moves uniformly up to the second impact, \[t=\frac{3d/5}{u/4}=\frac{12d}{5u}.\] Sphere \(B\)’s outward time is \(t_1=4d/(3u)\). Its return distance is \(2d/5\), covered in \[t-t_1=\frac{16d}{15u}.\] Therefore its rebound speed is \((2d/5)/(16d/15u)=3u/8\). Relative to the incident speed \(3u/4\), this gives \(r=1/2\). The second impact is strictly between the first impact point and the wall.

Part (c)

The wall changes \(B\)’s velocity from \(3u/4\) to \(-3u/8\). Thus \[L=\frac12m\left[(3u/4)^2-(3u/8)^2\right]=\frac{27}{128}mu^2,\] and \(\Delta p=m(-3u/8-3u/4)=-9mu/8\). The impulse has magnitude \(9mu/8\) and acts away from the wall.
questions.hint_html: The observed meeting point gives the elapsed time from \(A\)’s motion, before you know the wall coefficient.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find its return speed from the remaining distance and time.

questions.title: Two restitution coefficients linked by a parameter
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth sphere \(A\), of mass \(3m\), strikes a stationary smooth sphere \(B\), of mass \(m\), directly with speed \(u\). The sphere–sphere coefficient of restitution is \(e\), with \(0\lt e\leq1\). Sphere \(B\) then hits a fixed wall perpendicular to its path and rebounds. Its coefficient of restitution with the wall is \(7e/10\). Immediately after the wall impact, the spheres have equal speed magnitudes. No external force acts along the smooth horizontal line between impacts, and sphere radii are negligible in travel distances.

  1. Find their velocities after the first impact.

    [3]

  2. Find \(e\).

    [3]

  3. Find both velocities after the next sphere–sphere impact and decide whether \(B\) reaches the wall again first.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a=(3-e)u/4,\quad b=3(1+e)u/4\).

(b)

\(e=2/3\); each speed just after the wall impact is \(7u/12\).

(c)

\(v_A=7u/72,\quad v_B=7u/8\), both towards the wall; \(B\) reaches it next.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Take towards the wall as positive. The equations are \(3a+b=3u\) and \(b-a=eu\), giving \(a=(3-e)u/4\), \(b=3(1+e)u/4\). Both are positive, and \(b\gt a\), so \(B\) hits the wall first.

Part (b)

After rebounding \(B\)’s speed is \(7eb/10\). Equality of speed magnitudes gives \[\frac{3-e}{4}=\frac{7e}{10}\frac{3(1+e)}4,\quad 21e^2+31e-30=0.\] Factorising, \((3e-2)(7e+15)=0\). Only \(e=2/3\) is admissible. Then \(a=7u/12\); \(B\)’s velocity is \(-7u/12\). The wall coefficient is \(7/15\), also in \([0,1]\).

Part (c)

Write \(w=7u/12\). The incoming velocities are \(w,-w\), so \[3v_A+v_B=2w,\qquad v_B-v_A=\frac23(2w)=\frac43w.\] Thus \(v_A=w/6=7u/72\), \(v_B=3w/2=7u/8\). Sphere \(B\) is ahead, closer to the wall and faster than \(A\). Therefore it reaches the wall before another sphere–sphere impact or a wall impact by \(A\).
questions.hint_html: The equality after the wall is an equality of magnitudes. The two signed velocities have opposite signs.

marking_criteria.description_html: Equate speed magnitudes with reversed direction understood.
Select the admissible root and give the speed.
Use momentum and restitution for the new incoming velocities.
Justify the next event using direction, order and speed.
