questions.title: Two restitution values survive an energy measurement
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth sphere \(A\) of mass \(m\) and speed \(u\) strikes a stationary smooth sphere \(B\) of mass \(3m\) directly on a smooth horizontal surface. Their coefficient of restitution is \(e\), with \(0\lt e\leq1\).

Sphere \(B\) subsequently hits a fixed smooth vertical barrier. Its incident direction makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the barrier, where \(\tan\theta=4/3\); its coefficient of restitution with the barrier is \(1/2\). Immediately after this wall impact, before any other impact, the kinetic energy of \(A\) is \(25/156\) of that of \(B\).

  1. Find the signed velocities immediately after the sphere–sphere impact.

    [4]

  2. Find all possible values of \(e\).

    [4]

  3. For each value, state \(A\)’s direction after the first impact. Explain why the energy observation cannot distinguish the two cases.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a=(1-3e)u/4,\quad b=(1+e)u/4\).

(b)

\(e=1/7\) or \(3/5\).

(c)

For \(e=1/7\), \(a=u/7\gt 0\); for \(e=3/5\), \(a=-u/5\lt 0\). Kinetic energy contains no direction information.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Use the initial direction of \(A\) as positive. Momentum and restitution give \(a+3b=u\) and \(b-a=eu\). Hence \(4b=(1+e)u\), so \(b=(1+e)u/4\) and \(a=(1-3e)u/4\). The first can change sign; the second is always positive. Also \(b-a=eu\gt 0\), so the spheres separate.

Part (b)

The wall preserves the tangential speed \(b\cos\theta=3b/5\) and changes the normal speed to \(b\sin\theta/2=2b/5\). Thus \(B\)’s squared speed becomes \(13b^2/25\).

The measured energy ratio is \[\frac{\frac12ma^2}{\frac12(3m)(13b^2/25)}=\frac{25}{156}.\] So \(a^2/b^2=1/4\), giving \[\frac{1-3e}{1+e}=\frac12\quad\hbox{or}\quad -\frac12.\] The first gives \(e=1/7\), and the second gives \(e=3/5\). Both lie in the physical range. Neither sign may be discarded on the basis of an energy measurement.

Part (c)

Substituting into \(a=(1-3e)u/4\) gives \(u/7\) and \(-u/5\), respectively. Thus \(A\) continues forwards in the first case and rebounds in the second. The energy ratio depends on \(a^2\), so it cannot determine the sign of \(a\). The condition explicitly fixes the observation time before a later collision could alter either result.
questions.hint_html: An equation for kinetic energies can admit two physically valid signs for \(A\)’s velocity.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the wall speed factor from components.
Use the energy ratio including the masses.
Retain both signs when taking a square root.
Explain the loss of directional information when velocities are squared.

questions.title: A doubled angle determines a range of masses
questions.prompt_html:
Two smooth spheres \(A,B\) have masses \(m,km\), where \(k\gt 0\). They collide on a smooth horizontal surface. At impact let the positive normal direction \(n\) point from the centre of \(A\) towards the centre of \(B\), and let \(t\) be a perpendicular direction in the surface. Initially \(B\) is at rest, and \(A\) has speed \(u\) with components \(u\cos\alpha,u\sin\alpha\) in the \(n,t\) directions, where \(\tan\alpha=1/2\). After impact \(A\) moves at angle \(2\alpha\) from positive \(n\) towards positive \(t\), with speed \(v\).

  1. Find \(v\) in terms of \(u\).

    [2]

  2. Express the coefficient of restitution \(e\) in terms of \(k\).

    [4]

  3. Find the full range of possible \(k\). State what happens to the relative normal velocity at the upper endpoint.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=\sqrt5u/4\).

(b)

\(e=(5-3k)/(8k)\).

(c)

\(5/11\leq k\leq5/3\). At the upper endpoint \(e=0\) and relative normal velocity is zero.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Smooth contact gives no tangential impulse, so \(v\sin2\alpha=u\sin\alpha\). With \(\sin\alpha=1/\sqrt5\), \(\cos\alpha=2/\sqrt5\), we have \(\sin2\alpha=4/5\). Thus \(v=(1/\sqrt5)(5/4)u=\sqrt5u/4\).

Part (b)

Since \(\cos2\alpha=3/5\), the normal velocity of \(A\) after impact is \(3\sqrt5u/20\). Its incident normal velocity is \(2u/\sqrt5\); the ratio is \(3/8\).

Write \(U=2u/\sqrt5\) and let \(b\) be \(B\)’s normal velocity. Normal momentum gives \(U=3U/8+kb\), so \(b=5U/(8k)\). Restitution applies only along this normal: \[e=\frac{b-3U/8}{U}=\frac{5-3k}{8k}.\]

Part (c)

Because \(k\gt 0\), \(e\geq0\) gives \(5-3k\geq0\), so \(k\leq5/3\). Also \(e\leq1\) gives \(5-3k\leq8k\), so \(k\geq5/11\). Both endpoints are allowed.

At \(k=5/3\), the normal components of the two velocities coincide. Their tangential components do not: \(A\)’s remains \(u/\sqrt5\), while \(B\)’s is zero. Thus zero normal separation speed does not mean they permanently stick together.
questions.hint_html: Compare the incoming and outgoing normal components only after using the unchanged tangential component to find the speed.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the interval and interpret the endpoint correctly.

questions.title: A perpendicular deflection with unequal incident speeds
questions.prompt_html:
Two identical smooth spheres collide on a smooth horizontal surface. At impact choose positive \(n\) along the line of centres from \(A\) to \(B\), and positive \(t\) perpendicular to it. Before impact the velocity components \((n,t)\) are \[(2u\cos\theta,\ 2u\sin\theta)\quad\hbox{for }A,\qquad (-3u\cos\theta,\ -3u\sin\theta)\quad\hbox{for }B,\] where \(0\lt \theta\lt 90^\circ\). The coefficient of restitution is \(e\). After impact \(B\)’s velocity is perpendicular to its own initial velocity.

  1. Show that \(\tan^2\theta=(5e-1)/6\) and state the necessary restriction on \(e\).

    [5]

  2. Also, \(B\)’s outgoing normal component is half of \(A\)’s incoming normal component. Find \(e\) and \(\theta\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\tan^2\theta=(5e-1)/6\), so \(1/5\lt e\leq1\).

(b)

\(e=3/5,\quad\theta=30^\circ\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Write \(c=\cos\theta,s=\sin\theta\). Normal momentum gives \(a_n+b_n=-uc\), and restitution gives \(b_n-a_n=5euc\). Hence \(b_n=(5e-1)uc/2\). Smoothness leaves \(B\)’s tangential component equal to \(-3us\).

Perpendicular velocities have zero scalar product. Applying this to \(B\)’s two velocities, \[(-3uc)\left(\frac{5e-1}{2}uc\right)+(-3us)(-3us)=0.\] Divide by \(3u^2c^2\) to obtain \(3\tan^2\theta=(5e-1)/2\). Since \(\theta\gt 0\), the right side must be positive. Thus \(e\gt 1/5\), with \(e\leq1\). The same relation can be obtained by perpendicular slopes.

Part (b)

The additional condition is \((5e-1)uc/2=uc\), since half of \(2uc\) is \(uc\). Thus \(5e-1=2\), giving \(e=3/5\). Part (a) now gives \(\tan^2\theta=1/3\). The acute solution is \(\theta=30^\circ\).
questions.hint_html: The tangent components keep their original signs, even though the normal components may reverse.

questions.title: Equal final energies do not imply equal speeds
questions.prompt_html:
Smooth spheres \(A,B\) have masses \(2m,m\). Sphere \(B\) is at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. Sphere \(A\) approaches with speed \(u\) at an acute angle \(\theta\) to the line of centres, where \(\tan\theta=1/2\). The incoming normal component is directed from \(A\) towards \(B\). The coefficient of restitution is \(e\). After impact their kinetic energies are equal.

  1. Find the outgoing normal components of both velocities and the tangential component of \(A\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(e\), rejecting any value that is not physically possible.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a_n=(2-e)u\cos\theta/3,\ b_n=2(1+e)u\cos\theta/3,\ a_t=u\sin\theta\).

(b)

\(e=1/2\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Write \(U=u\cos\theta\). Normal momentum and restitution give \(2a_n+b_n=2U\), \(b_n-a_n=eU\). Hence \(a_n=(2-e)U/3\), \(b_n=2(1+e)U/3\). There is no tangential impulse, so \(a_t=u\sin\theta\), while \(b_t=0\).

Part (b)

Equal energies mean \[\frac12(2m)(a_n^2+u^2\sin^2\theta)=\frac12m b_n^2.\] Divide by \(mu^2\cos^2\theta/9\) and use \(\tan^2\theta=1/4\): \[(2-e)^2+\frac94=2(1+e)^2.\] Simplification gives \(4e^2+32e-17=0=(2e-1)(2e+17)\). Only \(e=1/2\) lies in \([0,1]\). As a check, \(A\)’s squared speed is \(2u^2/5\), while \(B\)’s is \(4u^2/5\); their unequal masses make the kinetic energies equal.
questions.hint_html: For \(A\), include the unchanged tangential component in the kinetic energy.

marking_criteria.description_html: Reject the negative root and give the physical value.

questions.title: Which way does the deflection turn?
questions.prompt_html:
Identical smooth spheres \(A,B\), each of mass \(m\), collide on a smooth horizontal surface. Relative to normal and tangential axes \((n,t)\), with \(n\) directed from \(A\) to \(B\), their incident velocities are \[(3u\cos\theta,3u\sin\theta),\qquad(-2u\sin\theta,2u\cos\theta),\] respectively, where \(0\lt \theta\lt 90^\circ\). Thus the incident directions are perpendicular. Their coefficient of restitution is \(1/2\), and \(B\)’s outgoing normal component is zero.

  1. Find \(\tan\theta\).

    [2]

  2. Find the total kinetic energy lost.

    [3]

  3. Find, in degrees, the angle through which \(A\)’s direction is deflected.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\tan\theta=9/2\).

(b)

\(108mu^2/85\).

(c)

\(\tan^{-1}(54/73)\approx36.5^\circ\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

For equal masses, the final normal velocity of \(B\), obtained from momentum and restitution, is \[b_n=\frac34(3u\cos\theta)+\frac14(-2u\sin\theta).\] Setting this to zero gives \(9\cos\theta=2\sin\theta\), so \(\tan\theta=9/2\).

Part (b)

Here \(\cos\theta=2/\sqrt{85}\), \(\sin\theta=9/\sqrt{85}\). The incoming normal velocities are \(6u/\sqrt{85}\) and \(-18u/\sqrt{85}\). Since \(b_n=0\), momentum gives \(a_n=-12u/\sqrt{85}\). Tangential components do not change and cancel from the energy difference. Hence \[L=\frac12m\frac{u^2}{85}\left(6^2+18^2-12^2\right)=\frac{108}{85}mu^2.\]

Part (c)

The components of \(A\)’s velocities are proportional to \((6,27)\) before and \((-12,27)\) after. The final vector is in the second quadrant, not the first. The change in direction is \[\delta=180^\circ-\tan^{-1}(27/12)-\tan^{-1}(27/6)\approx36.5^\circ.\] Equivalently, use the addition formula for tangent: \(\tan\delta=-(9/4+9/2)/[1-(9/4)(9/2)]=54/73\).
questions.hint_html: Zero normal velocity for \(B\) does not mean \(B\) is at rest; its tangential component remains.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the normal impact equations and zero final component.
Find the normal components including their signs.
Use the correct quadrant for the final velocity.

questions.title: Equal energies with a reversed normal component
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth sphere \(A\) of mass \(m\) and speed \(u\) strikes a stationary smooth sphere \(B\) of mass \(3m\) obliquely on a smooth horizontal surface. The initial velocity of \(A\) has positive normal and tangential components \(u\cos\theta,u\sin\theta\), where \(0\lt \theta\lt 90^\circ\). The coefficient of restitution is \(2/3\). The final kinetic energies of the spheres are equal.

  1. Find the exact value of \(\tan\theta\).

    [6]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\tan\theta=\sqrt{66}/12\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Write \(U=u\cos\theta\). Normal momentum and restitution give \[a_n+3b_n=U,\qquad b_n-a_n=\frac23U.\] Thus \(b_n=5U/12\), \(a_n=-U/4\). The normal component of \(A\) reverses, but its tangential component remains \(u\sin\theta\); \(B\)’s tangential component is zero.

The energy condition is \[\frac12m\left(\frac{U^2}{16}+u^2\sin^2\theta\right)=\frac12(3m)\frac{25U^2}{144}.\] Divide by \(mu^2\cos^2\theta/2\): \[\frac1{16}+\tan^2\theta=\frac{25}{48},\qquad \tan^2\theta=\frac{11}{24}.\] Since \(\theta\) is acute, \(\tan\theta=\sqrt{11/24}=\sqrt{66}/12\).
questions.hint_html: A negative normal component is permissible. Do not discard it before forming the full speed.

questions.title: A symmetric change of one velocity component
questions.prompt_html:
Smooth spheres \(A,B\), of masses \(2m,3m\), collide on a smooth horizontal surface. Let positive \(n\) be from \(A\) to \(B\), with positive \(t\) perpendicular to it. Their initial components are \[(u,0),\qquad\left(-\frac23u\cos\theta,\frac23u\sin\theta\right),\] where \(\theta\) is acute. After impact \(A\)’s velocity is \((-u/5,0)\). Sphere \(B\)’s speed is unchanged, its normal component reverses sign, and its tangential component retains its sign and magnitude.

  1. Find \(\cos\theta\).

    [2]

  2. Find the coefficient of restitution.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\cos\theta=3/5\).

(b)

\(e=3/7\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Normal momentum gives \[2u+3\left(-\frac23u\cos\theta\right)=2(-u/5)+3\left(\frac23u\cos\theta\right).\] Hence \(2+2/5=4\cos\theta\), giving \(\cos\theta=3/5\). The tangential momentum is already unchanged. Both signs of the normal reversal have been specified in the condition.

Part (b)

The incident normal velocity of \(B\) is \(-2u/5\), and its final normal velocity is \(2u/5\). Thus \[e=\frac{2u/5-(-u/5)}{u-(-2u/5)}=\frac{3/5}{7/5}=\frac37.\] The approach and separation speeds are both positive.
questions.hint_html: The reflection is of the normal component. A smooth impact cannot reverse the tangential component.

questions.title: Unchanged speed is compatible with changed direction
questions.prompt_html:
Smooth spheres \(A,B\), of masses \(m,2m\), approach one another obliquely on a smooth horizontal surface, each with speed \(u\). In axes \((n,t)\) at contact, where positive \(n\) is from \(A\) towards \(B\), their initial components are \[\left(\frac35u,\frac45u\right),\qquad(-u\cos\theta,u\sin\theta),\] where \(0\lt \theta\lt 90^\circ\). After the impact \(B\) moves perpendicular to the line of centres, and \(A\)’s speed is still \(u\).

  1. Express \(A\)’s signed normal velocity after impact in terms of \(\theta\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(\cos\theta\), explaining the sign chosen for \(a_n\).

    [3]

  3. Find the coefficient of restitution.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a_n=(3/5-2\cos\theta)u\).

(b)

\(\cos\theta=3/5\), with \(a_n=-3u/5\).

(c)

\(e=1/2\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Since \(B\)’s outgoing normal component is zero, normal momentum gives \(ma_n=m(3u/5)+2m(-u\cos\theta)\). Therefore \(a_n=(3/5-2\cos\theta)u\).

Part (b)

The tangential component of \(A\) remains \(4u/5\). Since its speed remains \(u\), \[a_n^2+(4u/5)^2=u^2,\qquad |a_n|=3u/5.\] After contact \(B\)’s normal component is zero. Separation requires \(0-a_n\geq0\), so \(a_n=-3u/5\), not the positive choice. Hence \(3/5-2\cos\theta=-3/5\), giving \(\cos\theta=3/5\).

Part (c)

The normal approach speed is \(3u/5+u\cos\theta=6u/5\). The normal separation speed is \(0-(-3u/5)=3u/5\). Therefore \(e=(3/5)/(6/5)=1/2\).
questions.hint_html: Use the separation condition to choose between the two signs produced by the speed equation.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use unchanged tangent component and the specified speed.
Choose the separating sign for the normal component.

questions.title: Parallel outgoing velocities after oblique impact
questions.prompt_html:
Two identical smooth spheres \(A,B\), each of mass \(m\), collide on a smooth horizontal surface. Let positive \(n\) point from \(A\) to \(B\) at contact, and let \(t\) be perpendicular to it. Initially \(A\)’s components are \((4u/5,3u/5)\), and \(B\)’s are \((0,3u)\). After impact the two spheres move in the same direction. The coefficient of restitution is \(e\).

  1. Find \(e\).

    [5]

  2. Find the total loss of kinetic energy.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(e=2/3\).

(b)

\(4mu^2/45\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(U=4u/5\). Normal momentum and restitution give \[a_n+b_n=U,\qquad b_n-a_n=eU,\] so \(a_n=(1-e)U/2\) and \(b_n=(1+e)U/2\). The tangential components remain \(3u/5\) and \(3u\).

Parallel velocities in the same direction require matching component ratios: \[\frac{b_n}{a_n}=\frac{3u}{3u/5}=5.\] The case \(e=1\) gives \(a_n=0\), but \(b_n\gt 0\), so it cannot satisfy the condition. For \(e\lt 1\), \((1+e)/(1-e)=5\), giving \(e=2/3\). Both normal and both tangential components are then positive, confirming the same direction, not opposite directions.

Part (b)

For \(e=2/3\), the outgoing normal components are \(2u/15\) and \(2u/3\). The tangential energies are unchanged, so \[L=\frac12m\left[(4u/5)^2-(2u/15)^2-(2u/3)^2\right]=\frac4{45}mu^2.\] This is positive, as expected for \(e\lt 1\).
questions.hint_html: Unchanged tangential components give the ratio of final speeds when the directions coincide.

marking_criteria.description_html: Translate parallelism using the unchanged tangential components.
Use normal components to form the energy difference.

questions.title: Two possible target masses
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth sphere \(A\), of mass \(m\), approaches a stationary smooth sphere \(B\), of mass \(km\), on a smooth horizontal surface, where \(k\gt 0\). The incoming speed of \(A\) is \(u\), and its velocity makes an acute angle \(\alpha\) with the line of centres, where \(\tan\alpha=3/4\). Its normal component points towards \(B\), and its tangential component is positive. The coefficient of restitution is \(3/4\). After impact the kinetic energies of the two spheres are equal.

  1. Express the outgoing normal velocities in terms of \(k\) and \(U=u\cos\alpha\).

    [4]

  2. Find all possible values of \(k\), and state whether \(A\)’s normal component reverses in each case.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a_n=(4-3k)U/[4(1+k)],\quad b_n=7U/[4(1+k)]\).

(b)

\(k=5/9\) or \(5/2\). There is no normal reversal for \(5/9\), and a normal reversal for \(5/2\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The normal impact equations are \[a_n+kb_n=U,\qquad b_n-a_n=\frac34U.\] Substituting \(a_n=b_n-3U/4\) into momentum gives \((1+k)b_n=7U/4\). Thus \(b_n=7U/[4(1+k)]\), and \(a_n=(4-3k)U/[4(1+k)]\). The tangential components are \(u\sin\alpha\) and zero.

Part (b)

Equal kinetic energies require \(a_n^2+u^2\sin^2\alpha=kb_n^2\). Dividing by \(U^2\), using \(\tan^2\alpha=9/16\), and multiplying by \(16(1+k)^2\), \[(4-3k)^2+9(1+k)^2=49k.\] Thus \(18k^2-55k+25=0=(9k-5)(2k-5)\). Both roots \(5/9\) and \(5/2\) are positive.

For \(k=5/9\), \(a_n=3U/8\gt 0\), \(b_n=9U/8\); for \(k=5/2\), \(a_n=-U/4\lt 0\), \(b_n=U/2\). In both cases \(b_n-a_n=3U/4\gt 0\), so both are separating, physically valid impacts. A reversed normal component does not make the second solution invalid.
questions.hint_html: The energy equation squares a normal component. Retain both mass roots, then check the signed velocities.

questions.title: A zero normal velocity identifies the mass
questions.prompt_html:
Smooth spheres \(A,B\) have masses \(m,km\), where \(k\gt 0\). Relative to normal and tangential axes \((n,t)\) at impact, with positive \(n\) from \(A\) to \(B\), their incoming velocities are \[(u,0),\qquad(-3u/5,9u/20).\] They collide on a smooth horizontal surface with coefficient of restitution \(1/2\). Afterwards \(B\) moves perpendicular to the line of centres.

  1. Find \(k\) and the normal velocity of \(A\) after impact.

    [4]

  2. Find the total kinetic energy lost.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(k=3,\quad a_n=-4u/5\).

(b)

\(18mu^2/25\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Sphere \(B\)’s final normal component is zero. Restitution gives \[0-a_n=\frac12\left(u-(-3u/5)\right)=\frac45u,\] so \(a_n=-4u/5\). Normal momentum then gives \(u-3ku/5=-4u/5\), or \(5-3k=-4\). Hence \(k=3\). The outgoing relative normal velocity \(4u/5\) is positive.

Part (b)

Tangential components are unchanged, so the energy loss can be computed from the normal motion alone. Initially the normal kinetic energy is \[\frac12mu^2+\frac12(3m)(3u/5)^2=\frac{26}{25}mu^2.\] Finally it is \(\frac12m(4u/5)^2=8mu^2/25\). Thus the loss is \(18mu^2/25\). The nonzero tangential energy of \(B\) cancels from this subtraction; \(B\) is not at rest.
questions.hint_html: Use restitution before momentum: the zero final normal component gives \(A\)’s velocity immediately.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find initial normal kinetic energy with the correct masses.

questions.title: One outgoing direction matches the other incoming direction
questions.prompt_html:
Smooth spheres \(A,B\), of masses \(m,m/3\), collide on a smooth horizontal surface. At contact choose normal and tangential axes \((n,t)\), with positive \(n\) directed from \(A\) to \(B\). Their incoming velocities are \[(u\cos\alpha,u\sin\alpha),\qquad(-3u\sin\alpha,3u\cos\alpha),\] where \(0\lt \alpha\lt 90^\circ\). The coefficient of restitution is \(3/7\). After impact \(B\)’s direction is the same as \(A\)’s incident direction.

  1. Find \(B\)’s outgoing normal component.

    [4]

  2. Find \(\tan\alpha\), and verify that the outgoing velocity of \(B\) points in the same rather than the opposite direction.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(b_n=(15\cos\alpha+3\sin\alpha)u/14\).

(b)

\(\tan\alpha=2\). Both components are positive; \(\mathbf v_B=(3u/(2\sqrt5),3u/\sqrt5)\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(c=\cos\alpha,s=\sin\alpha\). Normal momentum is \(a_n+b_n/3=u(c-s)\). Restitution is \[b_n-a_n=\frac37u(c+3s).\] Eliminating \(a_n\) gives \[\frac43b_n=u(c-s)+\frac37u(c+3s)=\frac{10c+2s}{7}u.\] Hence \(b_n=(15c+3s)u/14\). Its tangential component remains \(3uc\).

Part (b)

Let \(z=\tan\alpha\gt 0\). Matching direction ratios gives \[\frac{3uc}{u(15c+3s)/14}=\frac{s}{c},\qquad 42=z(15+3z).\] Thus \(z^2+5z-14=0=(z-2)(z+7)\). The acute-angle condition excludes \(z=-7\), leaving \(z=2\).

Now \(c=1/\sqrt5,s=2/\sqrt5\). Therefore \(b_n=3u/(2\sqrt5)\gt 0\) and \(b_t=3u/\sqrt5\gt 0\). This is \(3/2\) times \(A\)’s incoming velocity \((u/\sqrt5,2u/\sqrt5)\), so the direction is indeed the same. Both masses and the restitution coefficient are physically valid.
questions.hint_html: Parallel vectors may point in opposite directions. Check the sign of the scale factor after solving the angle equation.

marking_criteria.description_html: Apply restitution to the normal approach speed.
Verify a positive proportionality factor between velocities.

questions.title: A vanishing normal component and an energy constraint
questions.prompt_html:
Identical smooth spheres \(A,B\), each of mass \(m\), approach obliquely with speed \(u\) on a smooth horizontal surface. In normal and tangential axes, with positive normal from \(A\) to \(B\), their velocities before impact are \[(u\cos\alpha,u\sin\alpha),\qquad(-u\cos\beta,u\sin\beta),\] where \(\alpha,\beta\) are acute and \(\cos\alpha=3\cos\beta\). Their coefficient of restitution is \(1/2\).

  1. Show that \(A\) moves perpendicular to the line of centres after impact.

    [3]

  2. The total final kinetic energy is \(11mu^2/12\). Find \(\alpha\) and \(\cos\beta\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a_n=0\), while \(a_t=u\sin\alpha\gt 0\).

(b)

\(\alpha=60^\circ,\quad\cos\beta=1/6\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Normal momentum and restitution give \[a_n+b_n=u(\cos\alpha-\cos\beta),\quad b_n-a_n=\frac12u(\cos\alpha+\cos\beta).\] Subtracting yields \(a_n=u(\cos\alpha-3\cos\beta)/4=0\). Smoothness leaves \(a_t=u\sin\alpha\gt 0\), so \(A\) is moving, not stationary, and its direction is perpendicular to the line of centres.

Part (b)

The total initial energy is \(mu^2\), so the loss is \(mu^2/12\). Write \(c=\cos\alpha\), so \(\cos\beta=c/3\). The initial normal components are \(uc,-uc/3\), and final ones are \(0,2uc/3\), by normal momentum. Their energy loss is \[\frac12mu^2\left[c^2+\frac{c^2}{9}-\frac{4c^2}{9}\right]=\frac13mu^2c^2.\] Equating to \(mu^2/12\) gives \(c^2=1/4\). Since \(\alpha\) is acute, \(c=1/2\), so \(\alpha=60^\circ\), \(\cos\beta=1/6\). Both cosine values satisfy the prescribed angle domains.
questions.hint_html: Tangential energies cancel, which reduces the calculation to one cosine.

marking_criteria.description_html: Check the nonzero tangential component and interpret the direction.
Express all normal components in terms of one cosine.
Solve for the cosine with the acute sign.

questions.title: A loss fraction determines the target mass
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth sphere \(A\) of mass \(m\) and speed \(u\) collides with a stationary smooth sphere \(B\) of mass \(km\), where \(k\gt 0\), on a smooth horizontal surface. Sphere \(A\)’s incoming velocity makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the line of centres, towards \(B\), and \(\tan\theta=1/2\). The coefficient of restitution is \(1/2\). Exactly half of the total initial kinetic energy is lost in this impact.

  1. Find the normal velocities after impact in terms of \(U=u\cos\theta\) and \(k\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(k\), and show that a loss of \(60\%\) could not be achieved for any finite positive \(k\) with the same angle and coefficient.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a_n=(2-k)U/[2(1+k)],\quad b_n=3U/[2(1+k)]\).

(b)

\(k=5\). The loss fraction is \(3k/[5(1+k)]\lt 3/5\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The normal equations are \(a_n+kb_n=U\), \(b_n-a_n=U/2\). Eliminating \(a_n\) gives \((1+k)b_n=3U/2\). Thus \(b_n=3U/[2(1+k)]\), \(a_n=(2-k)U/[2(1+k)]\). Tangential components remain \(u\sin\theta\) and zero.

Part (b)

Subtracting the normal kinetic energies using part (a), \[L=\frac12mU^2-\frac12ma_n^2-\frac12kmb_n^2=\frac{3mkU^2}{8(1+k)}.\] Since \(\cos^2\theta=4/5\), dividing by the total initial energy \(mu^2/2\) gives \[f=\frac{3k}{5(1+k)}.\] Set \(f=1/2\): \(6k=5(1+k)\), hence \(k=5\). This gives \(a_n=-U/4\), \(b_n=U/4\), a valid separating impact.

For every finite positive \(k\), \(k/(1+k)\lt 1\). Therefore \(f\lt 3/5\). A loss of exactly \(60\%\) is a limiting value as \(k\) grows without bound, not an attainable value at a finite mass.
questions.hint_html: Use the total initial energy in the denominator; only the incident normal component is affected by the impact.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form the energy loss from normal components.
Obtain the loss fraction including the angle.
Check the final normal velocities are separating.
Distinguish the strict bound from its unattained limit.

questions.title: A deflection angle across the normal
questions.prompt_html:
Smooth spheres \(A,B\), of masses \(m,2m\), collide on a smooth horizontal surface. Relative to axes \((n,t)\), with positive normal from \(A\) to \(B\), their incident velocities are \((u,0)\) and \((-3u/5,4u/5)\), respectively. The coefficient of restitution is \(3/4\).

  1. Find the angle through which \(B\)’s direction is deflected, to one decimal place.

    [5]

  2. Find the total loss of kinetic energy.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\delta=\tan^{-1}(56/33)\approx59.5^\circ\).

(b)

\(28mu^2/75\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

If the outgoing normal components are \(a_n,b_n\), momentum gives \(a_n+2b_n=u-6u/5=-u/5\); restitution gives \(b_n-a_n=(3/4)(8u/5)=6u/5\). Thus \(b_n=u/3\) and \(a_n=-13u/15\). Sphere \(B\)’s tangent component stays \(4u/5\).

Before impact \(B\)’s direction is in the second quadrant, at \(180^\circ-\tan^{-1}(4/3)\) from positive \(n\). Afterwards it is in the first quadrant, at \(\tan^{-1}(12/5)\). Their difference is about \(59.5^\circ\).

The addition formula for tangent gives the exact check \[\tan\delta=-\frac{\frac43+\frac{12}{5}}{1-\frac43\cdot\frac{12}{5}}=\frac{56}{33}.\] The quadrant check above ensures that the acute value of the inverse tangent is the required deflection.

Part (b)

Tangential energy cancels. The incident normal energy is \[\frac12mu^2+\frac12(2m)(3u/5)^2=\frac{43}{50}mu^2.\] The final normal energy is \[\frac12m(13u/15)^2+\frac12(2m)(u/3)^2=\frac{73}{150}mu^2.\] Therefore \(L=(129-73)mu^2/150=28mu^2/75\). Including the unchanged tangent energy in both totals gives the same result.
questions.hint_html: The inverse tangent alone does not determine a direction: use the signs of both components.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the correct masses in the initial energy.
Use the outgoing normal velocities in the final energy.
Explain or account for unchanged tangential energy.

questions.title: Perpendicular incident paths with unequal speeds
questions.prompt_html:
Identical smooth spheres \(A,B\), each of mass \(m\), collide on a smooth horizontal surface. In axes \((n,t)\), with positive normal from \(A\) to \(B\), their incoming components are \[(2u\cos\alpha,2u\sin\alpha),\qquad(-3u\sin\alpha,3u\cos\alpha),\] where \(\alpha\) is acute. The coefficient of restitution is \(e\). After impact \(B\) moves perpendicular to the line of centres.

  1. Show that \(\tan\alpha=2(1+e)/[3(1-e)]\), stating why \(e=1\) is impossible here.

    [4]

  2. Given \(\tan\alpha=2\), find \(e\) and the speed of \(A\) after impact.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\tan\alpha=2(1+e)/[3(1-e)]\), for \(e\lt 1\).

(b)

\(e=1/2,\quad |\mathbf v_A|=4\sqrt{2/5}\,u\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The final normal component of \(B\) is zero. For equal masses, momentum and restitution give \[0=\frac{1+e}{2}(2u\cos\alpha)+\frac{1-e}{2}(-3u\sin\alpha).\] Thus \(2(1+e)\cos\alpha=3(1-e)\sin\alpha\). If \(e=1\), the left side is positive because \(\alpha\) is acute, while the right side is zero: impossible. Dividing for \(e\lt 1\) gives the result.

Part (b)

Substitution gives \(2=2(1+e)/[3(1-e)]\), so \(6-6e=2+2e\) and \(e=1/2\). Here \(\cos\alpha=1/\sqrt5\), \(\sin\alpha=2/\sqrt5\). Since \(B\)’s final normal component is zero, momentum gives \[a_n=2u\cos\alpha-3u\sin\alpha=-\frac4{\sqrt5}u.\] The tangential component is unchanged at \(a_t=2u\sin\alpha=4u/\sqrt5\). Hence the speed is \(\sqrt{a_n^2+a_t^2}=4\sqrt{2/5}\,u\).
questions.hint_html: Use total normal momentum when one final normal component vanishes; do not set that entire final velocity to zero.

questions.title: Recovering the complete outgoing speed
questions.prompt_html:
Two smooth spheres \(A,B\), of masses \(3m,2m\), collide on a smooth horizontal surface. Sphere \(B\) is initially at rest. Sphere \(A\) approaches at speed \(u\), at an acute angle \(\alpha\) with the line of centres, with \(\tan\alpha=3/4\). Its normal component points towards \(B\). The coefficient of restitution is \(1/2\).

  1. Find \(A\)’s outgoing normal and tangential components.

    [3]

  2. Find the speed of \(A\) after impact.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(a_n=8u/25,\quad a_t=3u/5\).

(b)

\(17u/25\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The incoming normal speed is \(U=u\cos\alpha=4u/5\). Normal momentum and restitution give \(3a_n+2b_n=3U\), \(b_n-a_n=U/2\). Hence \(5a_n=2U\), so \(a_n=2U/5=8u/25\). Smoothness leaves the tangential component unchanged: \(a_t=u\sin\alpha=3u/5\).

Part (b)

The two components are perpendicular, so \[|\mathbf v_A|=\sqrt{(8u/25)^2+(3u/5)^2}=\frac{u}{25}\sqrt{64+225}=\frac{17}{25}u.\] The normal component alone, \(8u/25\), is not the speed.
questions.hint_html: Solve the one-dimensional impact along the line of centres, then restore the unchanged tangential component.

questions.title: Timing a path between parallel walls
questions.prompt_html:
Two parallel smooth vertical walls \(X,Y\) are a distance \(d\) apart on a smooth horizontal surface. A small sphere leaves a point on \(X\) with speed \(u\) towards \(Y\), at an acute angle \(\alpha\) to the walls, where \(\tan\alpha=3/4\). It hits \(Y\), rebounds, then returns to \(X\). The two travel times are \(T\) and \(kT\), respectively. Treat the sphere as a particle for travel distances.

  1. Find the coefficient of restitution \(e\) at \(Y\) in terms of \(k\), and state the possible range of \(k\).

    [3]

  2. The displacement parallel to the walls, from the departure point to the return point, is \(4d\). Find \(k\) and \(e\).

    [3]

  3. Find the tangent of the acute angle the returning path makes with the walls.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(e=1/k\), with \(k\geq1\) finite.

(b)

\(k=2,\quad e=1/2\).

(c)

\(\tan\beta=3/8\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The incident normal speed is \(u\sin\alpha=3u/5\), so \(T=d/(3u/5)\). After impact the normal speed towards \(X\) is \(3eu/5\), and the return time is \(d/(3eu/5)=T/e\). Thus \(k=1/e\). A finite return requires \(e\gt 0\), and \(e\leq1\) gives \(k\geq1\).

Part (b)

The tangential speed is constant at \(4u/5\) throughout both stages. Therefore the parallel displacement is \[\frac45u(T+kT)=\frac45u\frac{5d}{3u}(1+k)=\frac{4d}{3}(1+k).\] Equating to \(4d\) gives \(1+k=3\), so \(k=2\) and \(e=1/2\).

Part (c)

The returning normal speed is \((1/2)(3u/5)=3u/10\); its tangential speed is \(4u/5\). Since \(\beta\) is measured from the wall, \(\tan\beta=(3u/10)/(4u/5)=3/8\).
questions.hint_html: Only the component perpendicular to the walls determines the time to cross the gap.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the normal component for the outward time.
Use the reversed scaled normal component for the return time.
Use unchanged tangential speed over both stages.
Use the angle measured from the wall.

questions.title: An energy ratio followed by an oblique wall impact
questions.prompt_html:
Smooth spheres \(A,B\), of masses \(3m,2m\), collide directly on a smooth horizontal surface. Initially \(A\) has speed \(u\) and \(B\) is stationary. After impact both move forwards and \(B\)’s kinetic energy is six times \(A\)’s.

Sphere \(B\) subsequently strikes a fixed smooth vertical barrier. Its direction makes an acute angle \(\alpha\) with the barrier before impact and an acute angle \(\beta\) with it afterwards. The barrier coefficient of restitution is \(3/5\), and \(B\)’s outgoing speed is \(\sqrt{13}u/5\).

  1. Find both speeds after the sphere–sphere impact, and the coefficient of restitution between the spheres.

    [4]

  2. Find the exact value of \(\sin(\alpha+\beta)\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v_A=u/3,\ v_B=u,\ e_{AB}=2/3\).

(b)

\(\sin(\alpha+\beta)=2\sqrt3/\sqrt{13}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The energy ratio gives \((1/2)(2m)b^2=6(1/2)(3m)a^2\), so \(b^2=9a^2\). Since both velocities are forwards, \(b=3a\). Momentum gives \(3u=3a+2b=9a\). Thus \(a=u/3\), \(b=u\). The restitution coefficient is \((b-a)/u=2/3\).

Part (b)

At the barrier the tangential speed \(u\cos\alpha\) is unchanged; the normal speed becomes \((3/5)u\sin\alpha\). Hence \[u^2\cos^2\alpha+\frac9{25}u^2\sin^2\alpha=\frac{13}{25}u^2.\] Thus \(25-16\sin^2\alpha=13\), so \(\sin^2\alpha=3/4\). Since \(\alpha\) is acute, \(\alpha=60^\circ\).

The final speed is \(\sqrt{13}u/5\), giving \[\cos\beta=\frac{u/2}{\sqrt{13}u/5}=\frac5{2\sqrt{13}},\qquad \sin\beta=\frac{3\sqrt3u/10}{\sqrt{13}u/5}=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2\sqrt{13}}.\] Therefore \(\sin(\alpha+\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta=2\sqrt3/\sqrt{13}\).
questions.hint_html: There are two different coefficients of restitution. The second impact does not alter \(A\)’s velocity.

marking_criteria.description_html: Translate the energy ratio with the masses.

questions.title: Reconstructing an impact from energy and angle
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth sphere strikes a fixed smooth vertical barrier on a smooth horizontal surface. Its incident speed is \(u\), and its speed after impact is \(v\). The acute angles its paths make with the barrier are \(\alpha\) before and \(30^\circ\) after impact. Exactly half of its kinetic energy is lost.

  1. Find the coefficient of restitution \(e\).

    [3]

  2. Find the incident angle \(\alpha\), to one decimal place.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(e=1/\sqrt5\).

(b)

\(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\sqrt{5/3}\approx52.2^\circ\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The energy condition gives \(v=u/\sqrt2\). Smoothness gives \(u\cos\alpha=v\cos30^\circ\), so \(\cos^2\alpha=3/8\) and \(\sin^2\alpha=5/8\). Normal restitution then gives \[e=\frac{v\sin30^\circ}{u\sin\alpha}=\frac{(1/\sqrt2)(1/2)}{\sqrt{5/8}}=\frac1{\sqrt5}.\]

Part (b)

From part (a), \(\tan^2\alpha=(5/8)/(3/8)=5/3\). The angle is acute, so \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\sqrt{5/3}\approx52.2^\circ\). The larger incident angle to the barrier is consistent with reduction of only the normal component.
questions.hint_html: Halving kinetic energy multiplies speed by \(1/\sqrt2\), not by \(1/2\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Use unchanged tangential velocity to determine the incident components.

questions.title: A right-angle rebound fixes the energy ratio
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth sphere strikes a fixed smooth vertical wall on a smooth horizontal surface. Its incident speed is \(u\), and its incident path makes an acute angle \(\alpha\) with the wall. The coefficient of restitution is \(e\gt 0\). The velocity after impact is perpendicular to the incident velocity.

  1. Show that \(e\tan^2\alpha=1\), and show that the fraction of kinetic energy retained is \(e\).

    [4]

  2. The impact loses \(3/5\) of the initial kinetic energy. Find \(e\), \(\alpha\), and the ratio of rebound speed to incident speed.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(e\tan^2\alpha=1\), and \(K_f/K_i=e\).

(b)

\(e=2/5\), \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\sqrt{5/2}\approx57.7^\circ\), and \(v/u=\sqrt{2/5}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Take tangent and outward-normal components. The incoming components are \((u\cos\alpha,-u\sin\alpha)\); the outgoing ones are \((u\cos\alpha,eu\sin\alpha)\). If the acute rebound angle with the wall is \(\beta\), then \[\tan\beta=e\tan\alpha.\] Perpendicular velocities give \(\alpha+\beta=90^\circ\), so \(\tan\beta=\cot\alpha\). Hence \(e\tan^2\alpha=1\), or \(\cos^2\alpha=e\sin^2\alpha\). Also, \[\frac{K_f}{K_i}=\cos^2\alpha+e^2\sin^2\alpha.\] From \(\cos^2\alpha=e\sin^2\alpha\) and \((1+e)\sin^2\alpha=1\), this fraction equals \(e(1+e)\sin^2\alpha=e\).

Part (b)

The retained fraction is \(1-3/5=2/5\). Part (a) gives \(e=2/5\). Then \(\tan^2\alpha=1/e=5/2\), so the acute angle is \(\tan^{-1}\sqrt{5/2}\approx57.7^\circ\). Since energy is proportional to the square of speed, \(v/u=\sqrt{2/5}\), not \(2/5\).
questions.hint_html: Resolve parallel and perpendicular to the wall. For a right-angle turn, the acute incident and rebound angles with the wall add to \(90^\circ\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Write the correct incoming and outgoing components.
Use perpendicularity to obtain the angle relation.
Use the retained rather than lost fraction.
Take the square root for the speed ratio.

questions.title: A smooth impact at the top of a flight
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is projected with speed \(u\) at angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal, where \(\tan\theta=3/2\). It moves freely under gravity. At the highest point \(A\), it strikes a small fixed smooth plane patch rising to the right at angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. The patch has been positioned so that this is its first contact with the particle. After impact the particle moves vertically upwards. The coefficient of restitution is \(e\), where \(0\lt e\leq1\). The particle then moves freely until its next highest point.

  1. Show that \(e\tan^2\alpha=1\), and express the speed just after impact in terms of the horizontal speed \(U\) at \(A\).

    [4]

  2. The extra height gained after impact is \(2/9\) of the height of \(A\) above the launch point. Find \(e\) and \(\tan\alpha\).

    [4]

  3. Find the magnitude of the impulse in the impact.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(e\tan^2\alpha=1,\quad V=U\cot\alpha=U\sqrt e\).

(b)

\(e=1/2,\quad\tan\alpha=\sqrt2\).

(c)

\(mu\sqrt{6/13}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At \(A\) the incoming velocity is horizontal, of magnitude \(U=u\cos\theta\). Along the upward-right tangent to the plane, smoothness gives \(U\cos\alpha=V\sin\alpha\). Thus \(V=U\cot\alpha\).

Along the outward normal pointing up-left, the incident component is \(-U\sin\alpha\) and the final component is \(V\cos\alpha\). Restitution gives \(V\cos\alpha=eU\sin\alpha\). Substituting \(V=U\cot\alpha\) gives \(\cos^2\alpha=e\sin^2\alpha\), hence \(e\tan^2\alpha=1\). Both speeds are positive, so \(V=U\sqrt e\).

Part (b)

The height of \(A\) is \(H=u^2\sin^2\theta/(2g)\). The extra height is \(V^2/(2g)=eu^2\cos^2\theta/(2g)\). Their ratio is \[\frac{\Delta H}{H}=e\cot^2\theta=\frac49e.\] Since it equals \(2/9\), \(e=1/2\). Part (a) gives \(\tan^2\alpha=2\); the plane angle is acute, so \(\tan\alpha=\sqrt2\).

Part (c)

The incoming and outgoing velocities are perpendicular, of magnitudes \(U\) and \(V=U/\sqrt2\). Thus the momentum-change magnitude is \[J=m\sqrt{U^2+V^2}=mU\sqrt{3/2}.\] Since \(U=2u/\sqrt{13}\), this is \(mu\sqrt{6/13}\). The impulse points along the normal up-left.
questions.hint_html: The pre-impact speed at the apex is not the projection speed. Resolve relative to the inclined patch, then return to vertical motion.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the magnitude of the vector velocity change.
Substitute the speeds to obtain the exact impulse.

questions.title: Equal arrival times at two perpendicular walls
questions.prompt_html:
Two fixed smooth vertical walls have traces \(x=d\) and \(y=2d\) on a smooth horizontal surface, where \(d\gt 0\). Two small identical spheres \(A,B\), each of mass \(m\), collide near \(O=(0,0)\); their radii are negligible for travel distances. At impact the line of centres is parallel to the \(x\)-axis, from \(B\) towards \(A\) in the positive \(x\) direction. Sphere \(A\) is initially stationary, and \(B\)’s incoming velocity is \((u\cos\theta,u\sin\theta)\), with \(\theta\) acute. The coefficient of restitution between them is \(1/3\).

After impact \(A\) first reaches \(x=d\) at exactly the same time as \(B\) first reaches \(y=2d\).

  1. Find \(\tan\theta\), and verify that \(B\) has not reached the other wall first.

    [4]

  2. Find the percentage of the total initial kinetic energy lost in the sphere–sphere impact.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\tan\theta=4/3\); at that time \(B\) has \(x=d/2\lt d\).

(b)

\(16\%\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Normal momentum and restitution for the equal masses give \(A\)’s velocity \((2u\cos\theta/3,0)\) and \(B\)’s velocity \((u\cos\theta/3,u\sin\theta)\). The arrival times satisfy \[\frac{d}{2u\cos\theta/3}=\frac{2d}{u\sin\theta}.\] Hence \(3\sin\theta=4\cos\theta\), giving \(\tan\theta=4/3\). At the common time, \(B\)’s horizontal displacement is \[\frac13u\cos\theta\,\frac{3d}{2u\cos\theta}=\frac d2.\] It has not hit \(x=d\), and \(A\) has no motion towards \(y=2d\).

Part (b)

Since \(\cos\theta=3/5\), \(\sin\theta=4/5\), the outgoing velocities are \((2u/5,0)\) and \((u/5,4u/5)\). Initial energy is \(mu^2/2\). Final energy is \[\frac12mu^2\left[\frac4{25}+\frac1{25}+\frac{16}{25}\right]=\frac{21}{25}\frac12mu^2.\] Thus the fraction lost is \(4/25\), or \(16\%\). This refers to the sphere–sphere impact only, before either wall impact.
questions.hint_html: Equal travel times refer to different distances and different velocity components. Check which wall each sphere reaches first.

questions.title: Two impacts inside a forty-five-degree corner
questions.prompt_html:
Two smooth fixed vertical barriers stand on a smooth horizontal surface. In plan view their traces are the rays \(y=0,x\geq0\) and \(y=x,x\geq0\). A small sphere first hits \(y=0\) at \((d,0)\), with incoming components \((-4u/5,-3u/5)\), where \(d,u\gt 0\). It next hits the other barrier. The coefficient of restitution is the same value \(e\) at both barriers. The first impact leaves \(4/5\) of the incident kinetic energy. Sphere size is neglected in travel distances.

  1. Find \(e\) and the velocity components after the first impact.

    [3]

  2. Find the position of the second impact.

    [2]

  3. Find the acute angle \(\beta\) that the outgoing path after the second impact makes with the barrier \(y=x\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(e=2/3\); velocity \((-4u/5,2u/5)\).

(b)

\((d/3,d/3)\).

(c)

\(\tan\beta=2\), so \(\beta\approx63.4^\circ\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At the horizontal barrier the \(x\) component is unchanged and the \(y\) component reverses and is multiplied by \(e\). Thus the outgoing components are \((-4u/5,3eu/5)\). The energy ratio gives \[\frac{16+9e^2}{25}=\frac45,\qquad e^2=\frac49.\] Since \(e\geq0\), \(e=2/3\), and the components are \((-4u/5,2u/5)\).

Part (b)

After the first impact, \[x=d-\frac45u\tau,\qquad y=\frac25u\tau.\] At \(y=x\), \(6u\tau/5=d\), so \(\tau=5d/(6u)\). Substituting gives \(x=y=d/3\gt 0\). The impact is on the specified ray, not its continuation.

Part (c)

Along the upward-right tangent to \(y=x\), the incident component is \[v_t=\frac{-4u/5+2u/5}{\sqrt2}=-\frac{\sqrt2}{5}u.\] Along the normal pointing up-left, it is \(v_n=(4u/5+2u/5)/\sqrt2=3\sqrt2u/5\). The second impact leaves \(v_t\) unchanged and gives \(v_n'=-2\sqrt2u/5\). Therefore the acute angle to the barrier satisfies \(\tan\beta=|v_n'|/|v_t|=2\).

As a check, the outgoing Cartesian components are \((u/5,-3u/5)\). Their direction is into the region between the barriers, away from the second barrier.

questions.title: Two perpendicular walls with different restitution
questions.prompt_html:
Two fixed smooth vertical walls have traces \(x=0\) and \(y=0\) on a smooth horizontal surface. A small sphere starts at \((d,3d)\), where \(d\gt 0\), with velocity \((-u\cos\alpha,-u\sin\alpha)\). Here \(0\lt \alpha\lt \tan^{-1}3\). It first strikes \(x=0\), whose coefficient of restitution is \(e\), and then \(y=0\), whose coefficient is \(1/2\). Assume \(0\lt e\leq1\) and negligible sphere radius for travel distances.

  1. Find the components of the velocity after each impact. Explain why the stated impact order is possible.

    [3]

  2. After both impacts the sphere moves at \(45^\circ\) to positive \(x\), and \(4/5\) of its initial kinetic energy has been lost. Find \(e\) and \(\tan\alpha\).

    [5]

  3. For a general acute incident direction, explain precisely when two perpendicular smooth-wall impacts produce a velocity opposite and parallel to the incident velocity. Apply your result to the coefficients here.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

After \(x=0\): \((eu\cos\alpha,-u\sin\alpha)\). After \(y=0\): \((eu\cos\alpha,u\sin\alpha/2)\).

(b)

\(e=1/\sqrt6,\quad\tan\alpha=\sqrt{2/3}\).

(c)

The two normal restitution coefficients must be equal. Here this requires \(e=1/2\), which is not the value in part (b).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At \(x=0\) only the \(x\) component changes, giving \((eu\cos\alpha,-u\sin\alpha)\). At \(y=0\) only the \(y\) component changes, giving \((eu\cos\alpha,u\sin\alpha/2)\).

The first wall is reached at time \(d/(u\cos\alpha)\), when \(y=d(3-\tan\alpha)\gt 0\) by the stated angle restriction. Afterwards \(x\) increases and \(y\) decreases, so the next wall is \(y=0\), at positive \(x\).

Part (b)

The final components are positive. A \(45^\circ\) direction therefore gives \(e\cos\alpha=\sin\alpha/2\). The retained energy fraction is \(1/5\), so \[e^2\cos^2\alpha+\frac14\sin^2\alpha=\frac15.\] Using the direction equation, the two terms are equal. Thus \(\sin^2\alpha/2=1/5\), giving \(\sin^2\alpha=2/5\) and \(\cos^2\alpha=3/5\). Hence \[\tan\alpha=\sqrt{2/3},\qquad e=\frac12\tan\alpha=\frac1{\sqrt6}.\] These satisfy \(0\lt e\leq1\) and \(\tan\alpha\lt 3\), so the event order assumed in part (a) is valid.

Part (c)

Let the wall coefficients be \(e_x,e_y\). Both incident components are nonzero. After two impacts the velocity is \((e_xu\cos\alpha,e_yu\sin\alpha)\). For this to be a positive multiple \(q\) of the reversed incident velocity \((u\cos\alpha,u\sin\alpha)\), both equations require \(q=e_x=e_y\).

Conversely, if the two coefficients are equal, both components are reversed and scaled by that same number. In this question \(e_y=1/2\), so reverse-parallel motion requires \(e=1/2\); the value \(1/\sqrt6\) found in part (b) does not have this property.
questions.hint_html: Each wall scales a different Cartesian component. Different wall coefficients generally destroy reverse parallelism.
